Article Title: In the 1970s, an Italian priest sold 12,000 piranhas to Europe; 55 years later, his proceeds have funded 350m bridges and an 800m airstrip on a remote Brazilian island
Article Text: An Italian Jesuit priest once turned one of the Amazon's most feared fish into an unlikely source of income for an isolated community. Giovanni Gallo organised the preservation and export of about 12,000 piranhas from Brazil's Marajó Island, with the proceeds helping fund bridges, a community dock, a cemetery and an airstrip, according to Brazilian academic research and recent reports by CNN Brasil. His wider work eventually led to the creation of the Museu do Marajó, a museum dedicated to the region's history and culture.The story dates to the 1970s, when Gallo arrived in Marajó, a large island in the Brazilian state of Pará. Brazil's National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage, or IPHAN, records that he came to Brazil in 1970 and reached Marajó in 1972. Gallo spent his first years in Brazil in other locations before settling in Marajó.Gallo eventually lived in Vila de Jenipapo, in the municipality of Santa Cruz do Arari. The community was isolated and lacked basic infrastructure. Houses were adapted to seasonal flooding, with residents relying on wooden walkways and elevated structures to move around during periods of high water. A historical account published by Ciência Hoje das Crianças describes the local bridges and walkways as precarious, while academic research records Gallo's efforts to address the community's infrastructure and economic difficulties.The solution he developed was unusual. Piranhas were abundant in the region, but Gallo saw a potential commercial use for the fish. According to a 2016 academic study on the social networks surrounding the Museu do Marajó, he established a laboratory where local women were taught to preserve piranhas. According to CNN Brasil, 12,000 specimens were exported to Europe. The proceeds were used both to pay the women involved and to finance community works.Those works were substantial for a small, flood-prone settlement. The academic research records 350 metres of wooden bridges, a community dock, a cemetery designed for the flood season and an 800-metre runway for aircraft.The piranhas, however, were only one part of Gallo's larger project. As residents began bringing him archaeological fragments found around Marajó, Gallo started collecting them. IPHAN records that the first objects came to him through local residents and that he gradually built a collection in Santa Cruz do Arari in 1972. Brazil's National Museums Registry said the Museu do Marajó began informally in Santa Cruz do Arari in 1972.The museum was formally associated with an organisation called O Nosso Museu de Santa Cruz do Arari, founded on December 16, 1981. In 1983, after conflicts surrounding the museum in Santa Cruz do Arari, the collection was moved to Cachoeira do Arari, where the institution became known as the Museu do Marajó and opened to the public in December 1984.The museum's approach was also unusual for its time. Rather than simply displaying archaeological objects behind glass, Gallo developed interactive exhibits known as “computadores de marca caipira,” or “hillbilly computers.” These handmade wooden structures used panels, strings, handles and mechanical elements to encourage visitors to interact with the exhibits. A 2024 doctoral thesis from the Federal University of Northern Tocantins described the system as a distinctive form of exhibition language built around local knowledge and community participation.Gallo died in Belém on March 7, 2003, aged 75, after spending roughly three decades working in Marajó. Academic and cultural sources describe his activities as extending beyond his religious role into community development, photography, archaeology and museology.
Article Summary: Giovanni Gallo organised the preservation and export of 12,000 piranhas. The proceeds helped fund bridges, a community dock, a cemetery and an airstrip. His wider work led to the creation of the Museu do Marajó. Gallo died in Belém on March 7, 2003, aged 75.

Article Title: An Australian council hired specialists to search two remote cemeteries for lost graves; the project has now located 658 unmarked burials, with 338 at White Cliffs and 320 at Menindee
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Specialists searched two remote cemeteries

658 unmarked graves identified

The discovery of 658 unmarked graves gives a clearer record of two cemeteries that have accumulated generations of burials (Image Credit: Central Darling Shire Council)

Why locating the graves matters

A memorial at White Cliffs

Preserving cemetery history for the future

A long-running search for lost and unmarked graves at two remote Australian cemeteries has identified 658 previously unmarked burials. According to Central Darling Shire Council, which funded and commissioned the project, specialist investigators located 338 unmarked graves at White Cliffs Cemetery and another 320 at Menindee Cemetery. The work was carried out to help identify and preserve graves that had been lost over time, while giving the council a clearer picture of the two historic cemeteries. The findings could also help with future cemetery management and heritage preservation in the region.Central Darling Shire Council contracted Hunter Geophysics, a company that specialises in locating lost, forgotten and unmarked graves, for the project. The work began in July 2025 and used specialist, non-invasive scanning technology to examine the cemetery grounds without the need for digging. The project focused on White Cliffs and Menindee, two communities within the Central Darling Shire in New South Wales. The area is known for its remote outback setting and long history, with cemeteries containing graves dating back through earlier generations of the communities.Rather than relying only on visible headstones or grave markers, the specialist search was designed to identify burial locations that were no longer clearly marked or recorded. This allowed investigators to map areas where burials were believed to exist even when there was little visible evidence at the surface.The completed survey identified 338 unmarked graves at White Cliffs Cemetery and 320 at Menindee Cemetery, bringing the total to 658, according to Central Darling Shire Council.The discoveries do not mean that the identities of the people buried at the sites are now known. According to the council, the passage of time means there are no details available about the individuals associated with the newly identified unmarked graves. The scanning project instead established the locations of the burials, helping distinguish them from areas where no grave was detected.The results provide a more complete picture of the cemeteries and give the council information that can be used to protect the burial sites from accidental disturbance.Finding previously unmarked graves is important not only for cemetery management but also for preserving the history of the communities in which they are located. Central Darling Shire Council said the project would help preserve the history and heritage of its cemeteries and towns. For local authorities, knowing where graves are located can also make future maintenance, planning and development work easier. Areas containing previously unidentified burials can be mapped and managed appropriately, reducing the risk of graves being disturbed during work within the cemetery.The project also adds to broader efforts to document the region's historic burial grounds. Central Darling Shire Council has previously worked on cemetery heritage projects intended to record information about graves and the people connected with the region's history. Council documents describe regional cemeteries as important repositories of historical information about the communities and individuals who lived in the area.The newly identified graves are also being incorporated into plans to recognise the cemetery's history. At White Cliffs, a large rock has been placed in the cemetery to provide space for memorial plaques, according to the council's project information.The memorial provides a way to acknowledge people whose burial locations can now be identified even though their names and other personal details have been lost. The use of non-invasive scanning was central to the project. Hunter Geophysics describes its work as using methods that can find and map buried features without excavation, including lost human graves and archaeological remains.The discovery of 658 unmarked graves gives Central Darling Shire Council a clearer record of two cemeteries that have accumulated generations of burials. While the project cannot recover the identities of those buried in the unmarked graves, identifying their locations provides an important step towards protecting the sites. The White Cliffs and Menindee survey ultimately turns areas of uncertainty into mapped burial sites. For the council, that information can support future cemetery planning, heritage conservation and respectful management of the grounds, while helping preserve a part of the history of two remote Australian communities.
Article Summary: Specialists searched two remote Australian cemeteries for lost and unmarked graves. The project focused on White Cliffs and Menindee, two communities within the Central Darling Shire in New South Wales. The work began in July 2025 and used specialist, non-invasive scanning technology to examine the cemetery grounds without the need for digging.

Article Title: In 2011, Judy Garland's former Bel-Air home sold for $5.2 million; after successive renovations, the 1938 house on nearly 2.7 acres changed hands again for $11.1 million in July 2024
Article Text: Judy Garland’s former Bel-Air home has changed hands for $11.1 million, more than a decade after it sold for $5.2 million. The 1938 estate at 1231 Stone Canyon Road was listed for $11.495 million in March 2024 before selling in July, according to property records and reports from The Real Deal, Realtor.com and Architectural Digest. The house carries a particularly strong connection to Garland’s early Hollywood years. She was 16 when the residence was commissioned, and 1938 was also the year she was cast as Dorothy Gale in The Wizard of Oz. Designed by celebrated architect Wallace Neff, the traditional-style home was created for Garland and her family and remains one of the properties associated with the actress’s rise to stardom.Set on roughly 2.66 acres, the estate combines the scale of an old Hollywood property with updates made by later owners. The 5,513-square-foot house has five bedrooms and seven bathrooms, with the grounds including a swimming pool and a separate writer’s cottage. The property is also located close to Sunset Boulevard and the Hotel Bel-Air, placing it within one of Los Angeles’ most established luxury residential areas.Its architectural character has remained an important part of the home’s appeal. The entrance opens into a grand foyer with a sweeping staircase and wrought-iron railing, while the interiors retain features such as hardwood flooring, storybook-style windows and traditional moulding.Later renovations introduced more contemporary luxury without completely removing the character of the original house.The kitchen was updated with modern appliances and a large marble island, while the adjoining breakfast area makes use of a bay window. The primary suite includes a fireplace, high ceilings, built-in storage and a dressing area. French doors and large windows help connect several of the living spaces with the surrounding grounds.Outside, the property has landscaped lawns, a brick-lined patio and a pool area. The detached cottage adds another layer to the estate and has been described as a writer’s studio. The combination of expansive grounds and a relatively intimate main residence gives the property the feel of a private Hollywood retreat rather than a newly built mega-mansion.Garland’s connection to the house goes beyond its construction date. Historical records identify 1231 Stone Canyon Road as the Judy Garland Residence, while accounts of her life place her there with members of her family during her teenage years. The house was part of the Stone Canyon Road area that attracted several entertainment-industry figures during Hollywood’s Golden Age.The property has also had a notable ownership history since Garland’s time. It sold for $5.2 million in February 2011, according to property records. It was then listed for $7.1 million in 2012 and sold for about $6.77 million that April. The home remained with the Chozen family until its 2024 sale.The 2024 transaction represented a substantial increase from the property’s 2011 sale price. After being placed on the market at nearly $11.5 million, the estate ultimately sold for $11.1 million, according to The Real Deal and the property’s sales record. The buyer’s identity was not publicly disclosed at the time of the sale.More than 85 years after Garland’s family first moved into the house, its biggest draw remains its connection to a defining chapter of Hollywood history. Unlike many celebrity properties that are heavily altered or replaced over the decades, the Stone Canyon residence continues to retain elements of its original architectural identity while accommodating the expectations of a modern luxury home.
Article Summary: The 1938 estate at 1231 Stone Canyon Road was listed for $11.495 million in March 2024 before selling in July. The 5,513-square-foot house has five bedrooms and seven bathrooms, with the grounds including a swimming pool and a separate writer’s cottage. Designed by celebrated architect Wallace Neff, the traditional-style home was created for Garland and her family.

Article Title: In 1945, a British submarine sank Nazi U-864 off Norway; 81 years later, authorities recovered 22 mercury containers from a wreck believed to have carried as much as 67 tons of mercury
Article Text:
The submarine’s final mission

Wreck found nearly 60 years later

Why mercury is such a concern

Robots reach the mercury cargo

The cleanup itself created a problem

Norway now considers sealing the wreck

In February 1945, the British submarine HMS Venturer sank the German U-boat U-864 off Norway’s Fedje island, killing all 73 people aboard. More than eight decades later, the wreck has become the centre of a very different problem: a potentially massive mercury cargo that remains on the seabed. In June 2026, Norwegian authorities recovered 22 mercury containers from the wreck during an underwater investigation, as per a report by Diario AS.According to Norway’s Coastal Administration, Kystverket, a wartime Japanese order found in British archives referred to 1,867 mercury containers intended for U-864. If the entire shipment was loaded, it would have amounted to between 65 and 67 tonnes of metallic mercury. However, there are no surviving loading documents that confirm exactly how much mercury was actually aboard when the submarine sank.U-864 was a German Type IXD2 submarine that was travelling from Germany via Norway towards Japan during the final months of World War II . Its mission, known as Operation Caesar, involved transporting specialists, military equipment and materials intended to support Japan’s wartime industry.Among the cargo was mercury, a strategically important material at the time. The submarine never reached Japan. On February 9, 1945, HMS Venturer located U-864 off the Norwegian coast. The British submarine fired torpedoes while both submarines were submerged, striking U-864 and breaking it apart. Norwegian authorities describe the encounter as a unique event in naval history: the first known instance of one submerged submarine sinking another submerged submarine. All 73 people aboard U-864 died, including two Japanese engineers. The wreck came to rest at approximately 150 metres below the surface, around 4 kilometres west of Fedje. It remained undiscovered for decades.U-864 was located by the Norwegian Navy’s vessel KNM Tyr in 2003. Investigations subsequently established that the submarine had broken into two major sections, with additional debris scattered around the site. The potential mercury cargo quickly became the central concern.Norwegian authorities say the Japanese wartime order discovered in British archives called for 1,867 containers. If all had been loaded, the mercury cargo would have weighed approximately 65-67 tonnes. But because the original loading documents have not been found, the figure remains an estimate rather than a confirmed inventory.That distinction is important. The wreck is believed to have carried up to 67 tonnes, rather than authorities having established that precisely 67 tonnes went down with it. What is certain is that mercury remains in and around the wreck.Norwegian government records say an area of approximately 47,000 square metres around U-864 is contaminated with mercury. Analyses and calculations have indicated that about 4 kilograms of mercury per year are leaking from the contaminated area.Mercury is a persistent environmental contaminant. Unlike many substances that degrade naturally, mercury can remain in the environment and move between water, sediments and living organisms. Of particular concern is methylmercury, a form that can be produced by microorganisms under certain environmental conditions. It can accumulate in aquatic organisms and become increasingly concentrated higher up the food chain.That is why mercury contamination around a marine wreck can become an issue extending beyond the immediate site. Norway has monitored fish and shellfish around U-864 for years. Authorities have also imposed precautionary dietary advice relating to seafood caught close to the wreck site. The Norwegian government's historical overview records that such advice was introduced in 2005 for pregnant and breastfeeding women and young children.The latest chapter began after Norway commissioned a new investigation of U-864. In August 2024, the Norwegian Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries instructed Kystverket to conduct further surveys of the wreck and surrounding seabed. The objective was to reduce uncertainty around the condition of the submarine, its mercury containers, the surrounding sediment and the feasibility of recovering some of the cargo.A seabed survey was carried out in May 2025. Kystverket used remotely operated underwater equipment to examine the wreck and its surroundings, including the keel structures where the mercury containers were believed to be stored. The next stage brought investigators directly to the cargo.In June 2026, workers focused on the bow section and exposed six keel boxes. In two of the forward boxes, they found mercury containers. Twenty-two containers were brought to the surface for examination. Investigators also found free-flowing mercury inside some of the keel boxes and in the seabed around the wreck. Kystverket initially estimated that roughly half a tonne of mercury had been recovered from the keel boxes. The operation also revealed how badly the containers had deteriorated after more than 80 years underwater.About 80% of the recovered containers showed damage and leakage, according to Kystverket. Several were marked “Almaden”, referring to Spain’s historic mercury-producing region and providing clues about the origin of at least part of the cargo.Recovering mercury might appear to be the straightforward solution, but the 2026 operation demonstrated why authorities are cautious. Working around the wreck can disturb contaminated sediment and potentially release mercury into the surrounding environment. Kystverket's assessment found that free mercury was present both inside the keel boxes and in the seabed.Its September 2026 report concluded that it is technically possible to reach the mercury containers using remotely operated underwater vehicles. But it also found that work around the wreck could cause mercury and contaminated sediment to spread. This has created a difficult engineering calculation: removing mercury could reduce a long-term pollution source, but the process of reaching damaged containers could temporarily increase contamination.After its 2025-26 investigation, Kystverket assessed two broad options: attempting to recover mercury containers before covering the site, or moving directly to covering the wreck and contaminated seabed.The agency concluded that both approaches could reduce environmental risk over the long term. However, it said recovering the cargo carried greater risk of mercury spreading during the operation and would be significantly more expensive than covering the site. Kystverket therefore recommended that the wreck and contaminated sediments be covered as a permanent environmental measure.The agency said a cover would provide a more predictable solution and lower environmental risk during implementation. It also noted that even if some mercury were successfully removed, the site would still need to be covered afterwards. That recommendation is not yet the final decision. Kystverket submitted its assessment to Norway’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, which will decide what action should be taken.
Article Summary: In February 1945, the British submarine HMS Venturer sank the German U-boat U-864 off Norway’s Fedje island. More than eight decades later, the wreck has become the centre of a very different problem: a potentially massive mercury cargo that remains on the seabed. In June 2026, Norwegian authorities recovered 22 mercury containers from the wreck during an underwater investigation.

Article Title: A Florida owner planned 52 ten-acre homesites across his 625-acre cattle ranch if the county would not buy it; after two years of talks, officials agreed to pay $7.8 million and stop the development
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Conservation Collier Initial Criteria Screening Report

Ranch was facing a 52-lot development

Two years of negotiations preceded the deal

Why the land attracted conservation interest

Cattle operation will continue for now

From potential homesites to protected land

A 625-acre cattle ranch in Collier County, Florida, is set to take a different path after county officials agreed to move forward with its acquisition rather than see the property move towards a large-lot residential development. According to Gulfshore Business, the county agreed to pursue the property for about $7.8 million following roughly two years of negotiations with its owner. The acquisition is intended to prevent plans for 52 ranchettes, each covering about 10 acres, along Oil Well Road. A 2023 Collier Countyfound that Wildflowerz Ranch scored 331 out of 400 in the county’s conservation assessment, reflecting its ecological value, wildlife habitat and connectivity.Wildflowerz Ranch is located along Oil Well Road, east of State Road 29, in eastern Collier County. The property stretches across both the northern and southern sides of the road and has historically been used as a cattle ranch. The development possibility involved dividing the land into 52 ranchettes, with each parcel covering roughly 10 acres. A 2024 real estate advertisement promoted 10.1-acre lots at the property, with asking prices ranging from $289,000 to $479,000.At a September 22 public hearing, attorney Rich Yovanovich, representing the owner, told the Board of County Commissioners that the preference was for Conservation Collier to acquire the property. If the county did not proceed, he said, the owner would move forward with development. That prospect became an important part of the county’s consideration as officials weighed whether to acquire the ranch through its Conservation Collier land-acquisition programme.The proposed acquisition followed a lengthy series of negotiations and changing appraisals. County records show that in September 2024, Collier County offered $6,700,500 for the property, based on the acquisition policy then in effect at that time. By December 2025, two new appraisals valued the land at $7.03 million and $7.99 million. In January 2026, county officials offered $7.03 million, representing the lower of those two appraisals under the policy in place at the time. The owner rejected that offer and countered at $12.8 million. The county later proposed $7.445 million for approximately 634 acres, using the average of the two appraisals.The revised purchase price was set at $7,813,564.70, after the owner agreed to convey an additional 14 acres to Lee County Electric Cooperative. Commissioners unanimously directed county staff to pursue the acquisition at that revised price. The county's current policy had moved to using the lower of two independent appraisals, which was $7.03 million. However, commissioners agreed to the higher purchase price, closer to the $7.99 million appraisal, citing the environmental value of the property.The ranch's development potential was only one part of the discussion. County officials also assessed the property's natural features and its position within a wider network of conservation lands. The property is within the Big Cypress Area of Critical State Concern and the Rural Land Stewardship Area Overlay. It is also adjacent to conservation lands and lies within the Okaloacoochee Slough, a freshwater wetland system covering about 32,000 acres across Collier and Hendry counties.The county's screening report identified freshwater marshes, pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods and mixed wetland hardwoods on the property. The land also provides habitat for a range of wildlife, including wading birds, caracara, gopher tortoises, Big Cypress fox squirrels and bonneted bats. Telemetry has recorded Florida panthers in the surrounding area.The Conservation Collier assessment awarded the property 331 of a possible 400 points. Its ecological value and ecosystem connectivity were among the strongest components of the assessment, while the report also evaluated human value, restoration and management potential, and vulnerability to future changes.The purchase will not immediately end the ranch's agricultural use. Commissioners also agreed to extend the existing cattle lease on the property through December 31, 2027. The ranch contains fencing, a cattle pen and chute area, a pole barn, a shooting berm and a covered shooting area. The September 22 county meeting agenda formally listed the Wildflowerz Ranch acquisition as an item concerning the proposed purchase through the Conservation Collier programme, including the proposed exclusion of approximately 14 acres for conveyance to Lee County Electric Cooperative. The ranch therefore remains an active agricultural property even as its longer-term direction shifts towards conservation ownership.The Wildflowerz Ranch deal illustrates how the county's land-acquisition programme can be used when privately owned property has both development potential and conservation value. Since Conservation Collier began in 2003, the programme has acquired more than 6,672 acres, according to Gulfshore Business. Its stated purposes include protecting water quality and wildlife habitat while creating opportunities for recreation and access to preserved land.For Wildflowerz Ranch, the proposed acquisition would prevent what could have become a 52-lot development and place the property under county ownership for conservation purposes. The proposed $7.8 million acquisition is also paired with an extension of the existing cattle lease through the end of 2027 while the county determines the property's longer-term management and use.
Article Summary: Collier County, Florida, agreed to pursue the property for about $7.8 million. The acquisition is intended to prevent plans for 52 ranchettes, each covering about 10 acres, along Oil Well Road. A 2024 real estate advertisement promoted 10.1-acre lots at the property, with asking prices ranging from $289,000 to $479,000.

Article Title: A Pennsylvania man started welding old car parts into sculptures in 1988; his Erie front yard now has a two-headed dinosaur and rocket ship
Article Text:
Image: Schaefer Family Page

How Richard Schaefer started making car part sculptures in Erie, Pennsylvania, in 1988

Meet Automan and the two-headed dinosaur: the most famous auto art sculptures in the yard

The attraction was formerly called Dick's Auto Art (Image: Schaefer Family Page)

More roadside sculptures made from automotive parts, from the rocket ship to the bumblebee and spider

Visiting Schaefer's Auto Art at 3705 Hershey Road in Erie: Location, hours and what to know

A Pennsylvania man named Richard Schaefer began turning discarded car parts into sculptures in 1988, and his roadside front yard in Erie has since grown into one of the region's most unusual local attractions. Visitors driving along Hershey Road will spot a two-headed dinosaur, a rocket ship, a bumblebee, a spider and a figure called Automan, all welded together from old engines, brake shoes and other salvaged automotive pieces. Here’s how the collection started, what you can see, and how to plan a visit, drawing on the artist's own family website.Richard Schaefer is an Erie native who first became interested in auto art in 1988, using welding and fabricating techniques and basic automotive knowledge learned from his father. The attraction was formerly called Dick's Auto Art and is now known as Schaefer's Auto Art.The raw material came from close to home. Schaefer's brother ran a junkyard called Denny's Auto Wrecking, and Schaefer spent a lot of time there, then began bringing car parts back to his own yard to work out how to weld them together. His first project joined the front halves of two Lincoln Continentals.The Erie News Now reporter was given a personal tour that began with Automan.Automan's body is built from an engine, a transmission and a drive shaft, and his shoes are made from brake shoes, a pun Schaefer clearly enjoys. Over the years, Automan has been dressed as a pirate, as a Halloween scarecrow, and on the day of the visit he was dressed as a golfer.Standing beside him is the two-headed dinosaur. It has spark plugs for teeth, an oil pan for a head and small wrenches for paws.The family website lists a bumblebee, a spider, a rocket ship, Automan and the two-headed dinosaur, and adds that there are more. The photo gallery also shows a Volkswagen spider, a yellow helicopter, a car set into the ground, and a suggestion box.Because the yard is a long-running project, what you see may change from visit to visit. Even so, the rocket ship and the dinosaur are the pieces that most often catch the eye of people passing by on the road.The sculptures sit in Schaefer's front yard in McKean Township, at 3705 Hershey Road. The family website gives the full address as 3705 Hershey Road, Erie, Pennsylvania 16506, and lists the hours as dawn to dusk. When a reader asked whether she could bring a child to see the art and whether there were set hours, the family answered that she was welcome and could come whenever. The stop is a must-see destination for visitors to Erie.The family manages the website, email and social media accounts. You can reach them at schaefersautoart@gmail.com, or find them on Facebook and Instagram under the name Schaefer's Auto Art.
Article Summary: Richard Schaefer began turning discarded car parts into sculptures in 1988. His roadside front yard in Erie has since grown into one of the region's most unusual local attractions. Visitors driving along Hershey Road will spot a two- headed dinosaur, a rocket ship, a bumblebee, a spider and a figure called Automan.

Article Title: A severely malnourished stray rescued in Mississippi in 2021 became a FEMA-certified search dog; years later, Canyon is 2026 Dog of the Year
Article Text:
From severely malnourished stray to FEMA-certified search dog

Training prepared Canyon for difficult searches

From Maui wildfires to Texas floods

A rescue dog helping others

Canyon named ASPCA's 2026 Dog of the Year

Award ceremony set for October 8

A severely malnourished stray rescued in Mississippi in 2021 has gone from months of medical care to working alongside emergency responders in some of the US’s most challenging disaster zones. Canyon was brought to the Hancock County Animal Shelter after being found as a stray, where he received extensive veterinary treatment before his intelligence and drive caught the attention of a search-and-rescue handler. He was subsequently placed with Category 5 K9, a programme that trains dogs for specialised search and detection work. After extensive training, Canyon earned dual certifications in 2023 for human-remains detection and wilderness operations. He has since deployed to major disasters, including the Maui wildfires, Hurricane Helene and the 2025 Texas floods, while also assisting investigations. The ASPCA has now named Canyon its 2026 Dog of the Year.Canyon's story began in 2021, when he was rescued as a stray in Mississippi and taken to the Hancock County Animal Shelter. He was in poor condition and required months of medical care before he was ready for a new chapter.During his recovery, however, those around him noticed that he had qualities that could make him suitable for demanding work.A handler later spotted Canyon's intelligence and drive and helped place him in the Category 5 K9 programme. The organisation works with dogs for specialised search, detection and service roles. Canyon underwent extensive training designed to turn his natural abilities into skills that could be used in real-world emergency situations.The transition required more than simply teaching Canyon to follow commands. Search-and-rescue dogs need to remain focused around unfamiliar surroundings, loud noises, difficult terrain and other distractions. They also have to work closely with their handlers, who learn to interpret changes in the dogs' behaviour as they detect scents.Canyon's training focused on human-remains detection and wilderness search work. He eventually earned certifications in 2023 through FEMA for Human Remains Detection and through the International Police Work Dog Association for wilderness operations.His physical abilities have also proved valuable during deployments. According to Christy Bormann, Canyon's handler, his size, speed and agility allow him to reach places that may be difficult or unsafe for people. His sense of smell enables him to locate human scent in environments where visual searches alone may not be enough.Texas A&M University has also highlighted the importance of veterinary support for its search-and-rescue canines. Bormann has described Canyon and another working dog, Connor, as family members and best friends, while stressing that their health and safety are essential to their ability to work.Once certified, Canyon began taking part in major search-and-rescue operations. His deployments have included the 2023 Maui wildfires and Hurricane Helene, as well as the devastating Texas floods in 2025.His work following the Texas floods was particularly extensive. Canyon spent more than 90 days searching along the Guadalupe River near Camp Mystic, where search teams worked to locate victims following the disaster. The prolonged deployment placed Canyon and his handler in difficult conditions as they searched large areas of terrain.Canyon's work has also extended beyond major disasters. Alongside Bormann, he has assisted with missing-person searches and homicide investigations. His specialised detection abilities can help teams search areas where investigators need additional scent-detection capabilities.Canyon's career has given his original rescue story a striking turn. He entered the animal welfare system as a dog requiring care and rehabilitation. After receiving that opportunity, he became a trained working canine involved in searches for people and human remains.The ASPCA specifically highlighted this transformation when announcing its 2026 Humane Awards. The organisation described Canyon as an example of what shelter dogs can accomplish when they receive a second chance and the opportunity to develop their abilities.For Bormann, Canyon's story also demonstrates why shelter dogs should not be defined solely by the circumstances in which they are found. His intelligence, drive and physical abilities eventually made him capable of performing specialised work in some of the most difficult environments faced by search teams.The ASPCA announced Canyon as its 2026 Dog of the Year as part of its annual Humane Awards. The awards recognise both people and animals whose actions have contributed to animal welfare or helped their communities.Canyon is among several 2026 honourees, including miniature therapy horses Aiden and Pearl, Kid of the Year Eloise “Lulu” Peck, farm animal welfare advocate Craig Watts, NYPD Mounted Unit Detective Kyle McLaughlin and Colorado Rapid Avalanche Deployment.The ASPCA's recognition comes after Canyon's years of work in disaster response and investigations. His path from a severely ill stray in a Mississippi shelter to a certified search-and-rescue canine has become the defining part of his story.Canyon and the other 2026 Humane Awards recipients are scheduled to be formally recognised at the ASPCA Humane Awards luncheon at The Plaza Hotel in New York City on October 8, 2026.Bormann has said she expects to continue working with Canyon for about two more years before he retires from operational work. After that, the search dog is expected to enjoy a quieter life away from disaster deployments.
Article Summary: Canyon was rescued as a severely malnourished stray in Mississippi in 2021. He required months of medical care before he was ready for a new chapter. A handler noticed his intelligence and drive and placed him in a search-and-rescue programme that trains dogs for specialised search and detection work. After extensive training, Canyon earned dual certifications in 2023 for human-remains detection and wilderness operations. He has since deployed to major disasters, including the Maui wildfires, Hurricane Helene and the 2025 Texas floods. The ASPCA has now named Canyon its 2026 Dog of the Year.
