NEW DELHI: The Indian Coast Guard , in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), seized approximately 526 kg of narcotics from an Iranian dhow in the Arabian Sea west of Lakshadweep, officials said.The Coast Guard said five Pakistani nationals operating the vessel were also detained during the operation carried out near Lakshadweep on September 25, as reported by news agency PTI.The drugs, valued at over Rs 3,000 crore in the international market, were seized after the vessel was intercepted during the operation.The Coast Guard conducted coordinated sea-air surveillance to track the suspicious vessel before launching a hot pursuit and boarding the dhow.The operation was carried out in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) to intercept the vessel. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine, while five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended.The dhow, its crew and the seized drugs were escorted to Mumbai under armed security for joint interrogation and further legal proceedings.The operation was part of coordinated efforts by the Coast Guard and Gujarat ATS to detect and disrupt suspected transnational maritime drug-smuggling networks.The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled through sea routes. The Coast Guard has previously conducted joint operations with Gujarat ATS and other agencies to intercept vessels suspected of carrying illegal drugs.In April 2025, the Coast Guard, along with Gujarat ATS, seized 307.5 kg of narcotics off the Gujarat coast, according to the Coast Guard's official record of interdiction cases.Several drug-interdiction operations have been conducted along maritime routes in the Arabian Sea, with agencies relying on intelligence inputs, vessel surveillance and coordination between maritime and land-based enforcement units to identify suspected consignments.The Coast Guard said the latest operation underlined its efforts to strengthen maritime surveillance and prevent illicit activities in India's maritime zones. The seized drugs and apprehended crew were brought to Mumbai for further investigation and legal action.
Article Summary: Indian Coast Guard intercepts Iranian dhow, seizes 526 kg narcotics worth over Rs 3,000cr. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine. Five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended. The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled.

Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: Student protests rock France with over 400 detained: Why are schools protesting - explained
Article Text:
File photo: A student walks past a burning bicycle next to the Baggio High School, blocked in protest of the government's release of next year's draft budget, in Lille, France

Students take protests beyond Paris

Civil servants join nationwide strike

Why the budget is at the centre of the anger

Poll Vote & Share your view Which area should receive greater priority in France’s upcoming budget? Education Healthcare Public Safety Infrastructure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

France was hit by a nationwide wave of strikes and student protests, with civil servants walking off the job and high school students blocking hundreds of schools as anger over budget cuts, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages spread across the country.The mobilisation came two days before Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's government is due to present its draft 2027 budget, which includes a planned €54 billion savings drive. The protests have added to pressure on the government as it tries to rein in France's finances ahead of next year's presidential election.The unrest was particularly visible at schools, where students piled up bins and barriers to prevent access. The education ministry said around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday, out of roughly 3,700 nationwide. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, according to interior minister Laurent Nuñez.​​At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured during Tuesday's unrest, according to officials.The school protests began in the Paris region last week but have since spread to cities including Lille, Lyon, Nantes, Marseille, Bordeaux and Rennes.Students have been protesting over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, poor school conditions and demanding timetables. At some schools, however, the demonstrations escalated into clashes with police.In Lille, rubbish bins were set on fire outside the Lycée César Baggio, while police used tear gas and batons after protesters threw objects. Similar confrontations were reported elsewhere, although many blockades remained peaceful.At the Lycée Arago in Paris, students blocked the entrance with bins while a placard reading "Macron explosion" was displayed. Outside the Hélène-Boucher school, protesters put up a banner saying "Fewer cops, More money"."We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally," final-year student Mael Breton told Reuters.Students have cited teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions as key grievances. “There are 34 of us in each class, and it’s just not feasible. The teachers are overworked,” a 16-year-old student told AFP, saying the education system was “completely broken.”The government's response has been mixed. Lecornu condemned violence around schools but acknowledged that students' concerns over the education system needed to be heard and addressed. Education minister Édouard Geffray said students had a right to protest but condemned violence as "indefensible".The student mobilisation coincided with a broader strike by public-sector workers, including teachers, healthcare workers and firefighters.Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France to oppose the government's budget plans and its proposed freeze on state employees' base salaries in 2027. The CGT union has argued that repeated pay freezes have eroded workers' purchasing power.Firefighters were among those taking part after a summer of major wildfires exposed concerns over resources. The education ministry said just over 11% of teachers and other school staff were on strike, while participation among other civil servants was below 10%.Transport disruption was limited in the morning, although the aviation regulator warned of possible disruption at some airports.CGT leader Sophie Binet said the government had 48 hours to reverse the planned spending cuts before the union considers further strike action."This summer, who was on the front line? It wasn't the billionaires, the big bosses or the shareholders. It was civil servants and working people. And how are they being thanked? By cutting their pay? The anger is enormous," she told BFMTV.Lecornu's government is trying to find savings as France grapples with a mounting debt burden. The proposed €54 billion savings package is aimed at bringing the public deficit down, while the government has also warned that public debt could reach 121.7% of GDP in 2027.France's public debt reached €3.595 trillion at the end of June, or around 119% of GDP, according to national statistics agency Insee.The cost of servicing that debt is also rising. France is expected to spend around €79 billion on interest payments this year, with the government projecting the figure could rise to €91 billion in 2027.The government is therefore trying to cut spending while unions resist pay restraint and students demand more teachers and resources for schools.
Article Summary: Around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, interior minister says. At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured. Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France.

Article Title: ‘Wake up’: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
Article Text:
The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections

‘Wake up’: Iran takes message to US voters

‘Death to America’ explained as attack on rulers

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that Iran's appeal to American voters will influence the outcome of the midterm elections? Yes, it will have a significant impact No, it will not influence the elections Possibly, but only to a limited extent 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians” as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran.The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes.IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the “harms” caused by its policies.The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administration’s behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message.The letter repeatedly attacks Trump’s justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iran’s nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes.“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said, echoing the letter’s argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals.The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iran’s unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz.The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington.The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbi’s remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material.The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iran’s political system: “Death to America”. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population.“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter says.The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washington’s political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict.The IRGC’s approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversary’s population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as “Hanoi Hannah”, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese side’s narrative.Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content.The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters.For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iran’s resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power.Meanwhile, Iran’s economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. The currency has repeatedly hit new lows since the war began.
Article Summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies. The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can leave families with difficult choices, including selling land that has been in the family for generations. Haupt faced this situation after her husband died and left her with hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines provided her with a regular source of income that she could use to repay the loans. Each turbine takes up less than an acre, allowing Haupt to continue farming most of her 160 acres. This means the same land provides her with two sources of income while only a small portion is used for the turbines. The payments can also increase over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments, helping landowners manage rising prices and other costs. For Haupt, the arrangement has made a significant difference. She has now paid off more than 80% of her farm debt while continuing to use the land for farming.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: Xi Jinping unwell? Chinese officials sought unusual long breaks during the US visit
Article Text:
President Donald Trump with China's President Xi Jinping

Hold room

Holding hands

BRICS summit

Fresh questions have emerged over Chinese President Xi Jinping's health after unusual arrangements made for him to rest during his recent summit with US President Donald Trump, reported by Wall Street Journal.People familiar with the planning told WSJ, Chinese officials asked the White House for a private room where Xi could rest between engagements and sought more downtime during his Washington visit.The most unusual detail was the request for a private “hold room” inside the White House's West Wing. According to the WSJ, Xi's wife Peng Liyuan was reportedly the only other person allowed inside the room, while even Cai Qi, a senior member of Xi's delegation and his chief of staff, was not permitted to use it.The arrangement was described by a former US National Security Council official as unusual compared with previous visits by foreign leaders.Chinese officials also turned down a planned working lunch between Xi and Trump on September 24, the only full day of his Washington visit, saying they wanted more time for Xi to rest. The decision created a roughly five-hour gap in the summit schedule.At Joint Base Andrews, footage reviewed by the WSJ showed Xi holding Peng's hand while using the aircraft's railing as he descended the stairs.Two days later, while climbing the National Archives steps alongside Trump and Melania Trump, Xi again held Peng's hand, with the WSJ reporting that he appeared to rely on her for support.The unusual scheduling was also visible elsewhere in Xi's itinerary. No official engagements were planned for him on the evening of his arrival following a roughly 14-hour flight from Beijing, while his visit to the US National Archives the following day lasted only about 10 minutes, far shorter than initially planned, according to the WSJ.The latest report has also brought renewed attention to Xi's health during his recent visit to India for the BRICS summit.During the opening session in New Delhi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly appeared to check on Xi, asking his interpreter, “Is it okay?” after the Chinese president appeared uncomfortable.Xi later skipped a gala dinner hosted by Modi for BRICS leaders and other dignitaries after attending the first day of the summit and holding a bilateral meeting with Modi.Taken together, the episodes have renewed questions over Xi's health, though no specific illness has been established. With Xi holding China's top political and military posts, any health concerns could have wider implications for Beijing.
Article Summary: Chinese officials asked the White House for a private room where Xi could rest between engagements and sought more downtime during his Washington visit. Xi's wife Peng Liyuan was reportedly the only other person allowed inside the room, while even Cai Qi, a senior member of Xi's delegation, was not permitted to use it.

Article Title: US engineers turn dredged river sediment into 3D-printed oyster reefs; six structures are now being tested in Mobile Bay
Article Text:
Image: US Army photo by Keesha Robinson

How the United States Army Corps of Engineers prints oyster reef domes

Six experimental 3D-printed reef structures in Coden

The Mobile Bay National Estuary Program’s newest artificial reefs were created using dredged sediment removed from the Mobile River shipping channel by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Image: Fox10)

How 3D-printed sediment reefs attract oysters and barnacles

What comes next for 3D-printed oyster reefs , a national engineering guide for oyster reefs

Every year, engineers dig millions of cubic yards of sediment out of the nation's shipping channels, and most of it has traditionally been treated as waste to be managed. In Mobile Bay, Alabama, the United States Army Corps of Engineers is testing a very different idea, printing that sediment into dome-shaped reefs to help oysters recover. Six experimental structures were placed in the bay in July 2026 and are now being monitored. If they hold up, the approach could turn navigation maintenance into a source of coastal restoration, and the Corps is finalising a national guide to oyster reef engineering.The idea gained momentum when Mobile District engineers were introduced to the Engineer Research and Development Centre's 3D printing technology. Researchers there collected fine-grained dredged sediment from the Blakeley Island Confined Disposal Facility and developed a specialised, printable mixture. Fox10 reports that the sediment was mixed with clay and printed by large-scale machines into dome-shaped structures. The domes have varied surfaces, openings and internal shapes that give a stable place for oyster larvae to settle. Elizabeth Godsey, who leads regional sediment management and Engineering with Nature work for the Corps, via the Engineer Research and Development Centre website, says the idea came from watching how oysters build reefs that filter and stabilise sediment.According to Digital Visual Information Distribution System, the current test builds on a pilot reef placed at an oyster farm on Mon Louis Beach, Dauphin Island, in October 2025 by the Mobile District and the Mobile Bay National Estuary Program. On 9 July 2026, the Mobile Bay National Estuary Program deployed six experimental structures in Coden. Three are made entirely of dredged sediment, and three are mixed with recycled oyster shell, so researchers can see which attracts more oyster growth. Henry Perkins of the same organisation told Fox10 that the structures will be monitored for six to 18 months to see what life they attract, how they hold up and whether they suit future restoration.Storms, shoreline changes and shifting sediment have contributed to habitat loss and fewer oysters in Mobile Bay. Early deployments are promising. Corps research biologist Al Kennedy says the printed domes are holding up against tides, and that barnacles and oysters settle on them as readily as on terracotta, the ideal reference material. The structures provide hard surfaces where none existed and can act as wave breaks that reduce energy, retain sediment and cut erosion. That matters because oysters are a keystone species in coastal Alabama, improving water quality, sheltering other species and easing shoreline erosion. Kennedy adds that scaling up could also restore capacity at the Blakeley Island facility.Future phases will dig deeper. Kennedy says the team plans to compare durability and oyster colonisation in all-sediment domes against domes of ten per cent oyster shell and ninety per cent sediment. It also wants to use a hopper to print continuously, print on site and on demand to cut transport costs, and find bio-inspired binders for the sediment. Beyond Mobile Bay, the Corps is in the final stages of publishing a national Engineering Practice Guide for Oyster Reefs. For the Corps, the aim is a sustainable cycle in which navigation maintenance directly fuels environmental restoration, redefining what beneficial use of dredged material can mean.
Article Summary: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers printed oyster reef domes in Mobile Bay, Alabama. Engineers used dredged sediment from the Mobile River shipping channel. The domes have varied surfaces, openings and internal shapes that give a stable place for oyster larvae to settle. Six experimental structures were placed in the bay in July 2026.

Article Title: Drew Barrymore’s grandfather once owned this Los Angeles estate; after Tony Scott bought and updated it, the property spent six years on the market before selling to her Charlie’s Angels director for
Article Text:
Built in the late 1920s by architect John Byers, the estate occupies just under an acre in Beverly Hills’ prestigious Post Office neighbourhood. John Barrymore, one of the celebrated actors of Hollywood’s Golden Age, was once its owner, giving the property an especially notable place in the city’s cinematic history.

A century of Hollywood connections

Spanish colonial character

Gardens made for entertaining

Some Los Angeles homes accumulate history so naturally that the property itself begins to feel like a Hollywood character. This Beverly Hills estate is one of them. Once associated with legendary actor John Barrymore, the sprawling Spanish Colonial compound has now changed hands for $14.7 million, adding another filmmaker to a property already woven into the story of American cinema, states a report by the Architectural Digest. The buyer is director and producer McG , who famously worked with Barrymore’s granddaughter, Drew Barrymore , on the Charlie’s Angels films, adds the online report.Built in the late 1920s by architect John Byers, the estate occupies just under an acre in Beverly Hills’ prestigious Post Office neighbourhood. John Barrymore, one of the celebrated actors of Hollywood’s Golden Age, was once its owner, giving the property an especially notable place in the city’s cinematic history, states the report.The seven-bedroom, 11-bathroom compound encompasses 6,976 square feet across a collection of structures. Rather than relying on a single grand residence, the property is arranged as a small private enclave, with a three-bedroom main house, two guest cottages, a one-bedroom bungalow and a two-storey guest house, adds the report by Architectural Digest.That layout gives the estate the feel of a secluded Hollywood retreat while offering plenty of space for entertaining and hosting guests, the online report adds.Much of the main residence retains the architectural language of its era, with exposed-beam ceilings, arched windows, French doors and richly detailed interiors. A formal living room features a mural-painted ceiling, while a wood-panelled library is anchored by built-in bookcases and a substantial fireplace.Another standout is the pub room, complete with a bar, dartboard and fireplace, creating a distinctly old-school entertainment space within the home. The interiors are not entirely locked in the past, however. Some of the guest spaces have been updated with a more contemporary aesthetic, including rooms featuring understated concrete walls. The contrast gives the compound a layered quality, balancing its historic Spanish Colonial architecture with more modern touches.Outside, brick and stone pathways connect the various structures, while loggias provide shaded areas for relaxing. The grounds also include a koi pond, fountains and a kidney-shaped swimming pool, reinforcing the estate's resort-like atmosphere. The property most recently belonged to Donna Scott, widow of filmmaker Tony Scott , who was known for directing films including Top Gun. Scott had acquired and updated the estate, but despite its provenance and extensive amenities, the property remained on the market for six years before finally selling.Now, its next chapter comes with another Hollywood connection. McG, who directed Drew Barrymore in both Charlie’s Angels and Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle, has become the latest custodian of a house whose history already reads like a film-industry family tree.Images Courtesy: Facebook and Architectural Digest
Article Summary: Built in the late 1920s by architect John Byers, the estate occupies just under an acre in Beverly Hills’ prestigious Post Office neighbourhood. John Barrymore, one of the celebrated actors of Hollywood’s Golden Age, was once its owner. The seven-bedroom, 11-bathroom compound encompasses 6,976 square feet across a collection of structures.

Article Title: Philip Rietveld assembled nearly 1,500 acres of Illinois and Indiana farmland over his lifetime; after his death in 2026, his family sold 23 tracts for $22.46 million, with one fetching $32,600 an acr
Article Text:
Representative image

A strategic two-state auction

The numbers behind the sale

Who bought the land

The man behind the portfolio

Why prices were so high

How the sale compares to statewide averages

A legacy that changes hands

Over a lifetime of careful acquisitions, Philip Rietveld built a portfolio of nearly 1,500 acres of productive farmland across Illinois and Indiana. After his death in 2026, his family moved to sell the holdings through a two-day, two-state auction that drew bidders from seven states. The 23 tracts changed hands for a combined $22.46 million, with one 39.9-acre Indiana parcel commanding a striking $32,600 per acre, according to reporting on the sale by Agriculture.com. Read on to know more about it here:The sale was handled by Geswein Farm and Land, a brokerage with nearly five decades of experience in agricultural real estate. Rather than listing all the parcels in a single marathon event, the firm split the auction across two days and two states in the first week of September. This approach was designed to give each local market its own moment while keeping the entire portfolio in view as one major regional land event.Johnny Klemme of Geswein said the strategy aimed to reduce buyer fatigue and keep attention focused on the land, according to Agriculture.com. By separating the Illinois and Indiana portions, the company hoped to encourage competitive bidding in each state without overwhelming participants.Klemme described the event as one of the largest in the firm’s history and said the results exceeded even their most optimistic expectations, as per the report.In total, 1,477.5 acres sold for $22,458,078, producing a combined average of $15,200 per acre across the portfolio. The Illinois side included 15 tracts covering 856.84 acres, which generated 197 bids and brought $9,479,881, or about $11,064 per acre. Prices on those parcels ranged from $8,600 to $16,100 per acre, reflecting differences in location, size, and soil productivity.The Indiana portion was smaller in acreage but far more intense in bidding activity. Eight tracts totaling 620.72 acres attracted 539 bids and sold for $12,978,197, or roughly $20,908 per acre.Individual Indiana prices ranged from $16,600 to the headline $32,600 per acre. Klemme noted, as per the report, that every Indiana tract sold at the high end of what the team had anticipated, with the top result standing out even in a strong market.The auction drew 82 registered bidders from Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Maryland, North Carolina, and Washington. Despite the national interest, no institutional investors purchased any of the tracts. One regional land investment group acquired property on the Illinois side, while the remaining buyers were largely local or regional farmers and landowners looking to expand their operations or secure long-term assets, as per the report. In the end, 13 buyers purchased the 15 Illinois tracts, and just two buyers acquired all eight Indiana tracts. Klemme said these were mostly regional participants who understood the local landscape and were willing to bid aggressively, the report suggested. Their knowledge of nearby development, rezoning potential, and farm performance likely influenced how they valued each parcel.The land was held in the Philip Rietveld Trust. According to Klemme, Rietveld assembled the holdings over his lifetime before passing away earlier in 2026. Though he did not farm the ground himself, he was intentional about where he bought and had a clear sense of what made a high-quality farm. His tenants maintained the properties well, many of them renting the same fields for years, according to the report by Agriculture.com.The farms shared several attractive features, including paved road frontage, locations near towns, and similar soil profiles and productivity indexes. That consistency made the portfolio easier to market as a cohesive set of assets while still allowing each tract to be evaluated on its own merits. For buyers, the combination of location, maintenance and soil quality made for an attractive package.According to the report by Agriculture.com, Klemme said fundamentals such as strong locations, well-maintained fields and productive soils were key reasons for the sale’s performance. He also cited less tangible factors, such as local knowledge about future development or nearby land-use changes that may not be as obvious to outsiders. In transitional areas, farmland values are not always based on traditional agricultural economics alone. Buyers often view farmland through multiple lenses, including farm expansion, income generation, inflation protection, long-term wealth preservation, development potential and legacy ownership. Unlike many other assets, farmland is finite, which adds to its appeal for families seeking to build or preserve wealth across generations. Klemme noted that each sale represents the closing of one family’s chapter and the start of another’s.The Rietveld farms sold above statewide averages in both Illinois and Indiana. According to the National Agricultural Statistics Service, Illinois farm real estate averaged $9,250 per acre in 2026, up 3.6 percent from the previous year and marking the sixth consecutive year of at least a 2.4 percent annual increase. The Illinois tracts in this auction, with prices from $8,600 to $16,100 per acre, sat at or above that benchmark depending on location and quality. In Indiana, Purdue University’s Farmland Values and Cash Rent Survey showed more mixed results in 2026. Top-quality farmland averaged $14,909 per acre, up slightly from 2025, while average-quality and poor-quality land saw modest declines. The Indiana tracts in the Rietveld sale, ranging from $16,600 to $32,600 per acre, traded well above those statewide figures, reflecting their proximity to Chicago, strong soils, and competitive local demand.For the Rietveld family, the auction marked the end of a long chapter in which Philip Rietveld carefully built a geographically balanced portfolio of Midwestern farmland. For the buyers, it represented an opportunity to acquire well-located, productive ground in a market where supply is limited and demand remains firm. The sale underscores how farmland continues to function as both a working asset and a store of value for families and investors alike.
Article Summary: Philip Rietveld built a portfolio of nearly 1,500 acres of productive farmland across Illinois and Indiana. After his death in 2026, his family moved to sell the holdings through a two-day, two-state auction. The 23 tracts changed hands for a combined $22.46 million, with one 39.9-acre Indiana parcel commanding $32,600 per acre.

Article Title: In 1975, lawyer John Swenson ordered rocambole garlic out of curiosity; decades later, his collection helped spark America's Garlic Revolution
Article Text:
PC: Seed Savers Exchange

How John turned his curiosity into detailed historical research

How John’s rocambole garlic discovery led to decades of seed saving

How a 1989 USDA mission brought 120 garlic varieties back

PC: Seed Savers Exchange

How John Swenson helped spark America’s Garlic Revolution

In 1975, while practising as a lawyer, John Swenson became interested in alliums while flipping through a seed catalogue. Out of sheer curiosity, he ordered rocambole garlic bulbs and never looked back. According to Seed Savers Exchange, he became a lifetime member in 1985, listed 133 varieties in its Yearbook over 33 years and donated 150 varieties to its seed bank collection. In 1989, he joined a USDA team on a mission through Russia and Central Asia, which returned with 120 varieties of garlic. His sharing of some of those varieties helped spark a "Garlic Revolution" in the United States seed trade.John Swenson graduated magna cum laude from Dartmouth College in 1950 with majors in philosophy and sociology before attending Northwestern University School of Law. The organisation describes his successful career in law as one that "translated seamlessly into every aspect of his life". It also credits him with a relentless pursuit of truth and accuracy and a wide-ranging intellect.In the late 1980s, John turned those qualities and his passion for alliums towards a multi-year project on the etymology of the term Chicago. He had come to realise that the common story, that the city was named after a common prairie onion, might be false.The organisation says he researched regional history methodically, teaching himself to read 11 Native American languages along the way.John's interest in alliums began in 1975 while he was flipping through a seed catalogue. He ordered rocambole garlic bulbs "out of sheer curiosity". The organisation notes that later that same year he first read about Seed Savers Exchange, then called True Seed Exchange, in Organic Gardening magazine.John officially became a listed member in 1984 and a lifetime member in 1985. Over 33 years, it records, he listed 133 varieties in the Yearbook and donated 150 varieties to the organisation's seed bank collection. He also acted as an advisor to Seed Savers Exchange for several years. The organisation adds that John mentioned he often ate 12 varieties of garlic in a day.John joined a USDA team of biologists in 1989 on a collections mission through Russia and Central Asia. The team searched remote hillsides and bustling marketplaces for every garlic, onion, shallot and carrot possible. Although the team entered what was then the USSR fully accredited, foreign agencies often treated its members with suspicion.Seed Savers Exchange states that John, who stood 6'2", remembered being assigned the smallest seat on a flight from Moscow to Ashgabat. He recalled that the only flights available to Americans were at night. "It was like a military drill," he said, laughing. "They didn't want us American spies to fly out during the daytime because we could see." The organisation reports that the team returned with 120 varieties of garlic alone.USDA materials are generally kept in their collection, but John procured samples from as many of the USSR accessions as possible and grew them all in his backyard. He later shared his entire collection with Seed Savers Exchange, which became the foundation of the organisation's garlic collection. He also listed many of his garlic varieties in the Exchange and later sold much of his collection to Filaree Farms in Washington. Of his approach, John said: "My attitude is, what good is knowledge if you can't share it?"His efforts to share helped spark a "Garlic Revolution". The number of garlic varieties available in the United States seed trade rose from 18 in 1987 to 274 by 2004. In 1991, it adds, John wrote "Chicagoua/Chicago: The Origin, Meaning, and Etymology of a Place Name" for Illinois Historic Journal, after finding the diary of Henri Joutel, a French soldier who travelled through the area in 1687. Even in retirement, John continued to help people track down varieties and volunteered with the Chicago Botanic Garden. "I have an ongoing project of selecting and donating unusual seeds," he explained. John Swenson passed away peacefully in his sleep on 9 July 2024, aged 95.
Article Summary: John Swenson's interest in alliums began in 1975 while flipping through a seed catalogue. He ordered rocambole garlic bulbs "out of sheer curiosity" In 1989, he joined a USDA team on a mission through Russia and Central Asia, which returned with 120 varieties of garlic. His sharing of some of those varieties helped spark a "Garlic Revolution" in the United States seed trade.

Article Title: Beth Feeback paid $9.99 for a North Carolina thrift-store painting she wanted to cover with cats; it proved to be an Ilya Bolotowsky work and sold at Sotheby's for $34,375, including fees
Article Text: A North Carolina artist once walked into a Goodwill store looking for inexpensive material for her own artwork and walked out with what would turn out to be a valuable piece of American abstraction. Beth Feeback paid just $9.99 for a large painting in 2012, not because she admired the artwork, but because she wanted to reuse its canvas for one of her own paintings featuring cats. Months later, a friend's suggestion to check the markings on the back changed the fate of the seemingly ordinary thrift-store find, according to a report by ABC News.The painting turned out to be “Vertical Diamond” by Ilya Bolotowsky, a Russian-born American abstract artist whose work is held by major museums. It was subsequently authenticated and offered at Sotheby's in New York, where it sold for about $27,000 at auction. With the buyer's premium included, Sotheby's listed the final price as $34,375.The extraordinary discovery began with a purchase that Feeback had no reason to regard as an art investment. According to ABC News, Feeback, who lived in Concord, North Carolina, bought the painting in April 2012. She was not particularly drawn to its abstract style.Instead, she saw the large canvas as useful material for her own work. Her speciality was painting cat portraits, and she intended to paint over the existing artwork and create something of her own. The painting reportedly sat on the floor of her art studio for several months.Then a friend urged Feeback to inspect the labels and markings on the back before putting a brush to the canvas.That small piece of advice proved crucial. Feeback discovered the name Ilya Bolotowsky associated with the work and began researching the artist. The painting was identified as “Vertical Diamond,” a geometric abstract work. Rather than covering it with cat portraits, she decided to have it examined and pursue a sale.Contemporary reports said Sotheby's estimated that the painting could sell for between $15,000 and $20,000. That estimate was already dramatically higher than the $9.99 Feeback had paid, but the final result went beyond it. When the painting went under the hammer in September 2012, Feeback watched the auction remotely with family and friends. She had concerns that it might not sell at all, particularly because some other works at the auction were selling below estimates or failing to find buyers. Instead, the Bolotowsky painting attracted a successful bid of roughly $27,000.Sotheby's reported the total sale price as $34,375, a figure that included the premium paid by the buyer on top of the hammer price. ABC News specifically clarified the distinction, making the $34,375 figure different from the amount Feeback actually received from the sale.For Feeback, the result transformed a $9.99 purchase into a significant financial windfall. She told ABC News that she and her husband planned to use the money for long-delayed improvements to their home and to pay down debts. She also joked about the unlikely journey of the artwork: instead of painting cats over Bolotowsky's work, she planned to create her own versions inspired by “Vertical Diamond,” this time incorporating large cat heads.The artist behind the thrift-store discovery had a significant place in the history of American abstraction. Ilya Bolotowsky was born in St Petersburg, Russia, in 1907 and died in New York in 1981. The Smithsonian's Archives of American Art describes him as a Russian-American abstract painter. He immigrated to the United States in 1923 and studied at the National Academy of Design. Bolotowsky became closely associated with geometric abstraction and was a founding member of the American Abstract Artists, an organisation formed to promote abstract art in the United States. His work was strongly influenced by Dutch artist Piet Mondrian and the principles of geometric abstraction. Smithsonian American Art MuseumHis career also included work under the federal art programmes of the 1930s and teaching positions at institutions including Black Mountain College, the University of Wyoming and Brooklyn College. The Smithsonian records his involvement with the Public Works of Art Project and the Works Progress Administration's Federal Art Project.Bolotowsky's work later received institutional recognition, including a 1974 retrospective at New York's Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, according to museum and gallery records. “Vertical Diamond” itself is recorded as a 1966 oil-on-canvas work. Art-market records identify its September 21, 2012 sale and its $34,375 result, consistent with the contemporary reports of Feeback's discovery.The provenance of the painting also helped explain why such a significant work could eventually end up in a thrift store. Reports noted a Weatherspoon Art Museum sticker on the back, connecting the canvas to the University of North Carolina at Greensboro's museum. Contemporary accounts said museum records indicated that Burlington Industries had loaned the painting to the Weatherspoon for an exhibition in 1979. For Feeback, however, none of that history was apparent when she first saw the painting.At Goodwill, it was simply a large canvas she could buy for less than $10. Had her friend's warning come too late, the artwork might have been painted over and its identity lost. Instead, a quick check of the label led to an artist, a title, an auction and a final reported price of $34,375 including the buyer's premium.
