Article Title: Cornell rape victim ‘failed’ by people bound to protect her: New York governor
Article Text: NEW YORK: The woman who accused members of a Cornell University fraternity of gang rape was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including campus police and county prosecutor, New York governor Kathy Hochul said Friday.Hochul said at a news conference that she decided to appoint attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the investigation after learning “troubling details” about how authorities have handled the woman’s claims thus far, including that the district attorney closed the case without having anyone interview the accuser or anyone else involved in the alleged attack.“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” Hochul said. “This woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”The probe was closed without charges in 2024, but Van Houten reopened it on Monday after the woman sued seven former Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others. The lawsuit alleges she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sexual acts by several men while partially or entirely incapacitated.Lawyers for two defendants denied they participated in a sexual assault.Van Houten, who was removed from the case, backed James’ appointment but said the university had not provided the full picture. James said her office would review evidence, interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted, adding that the investigation could take months.
Article Summary: New York governor Kathy Hochul appointed attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the investigation. The probe was closed without charges in 2024, but Van Houten reopened it on Monday after the woman sued seven former Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others.

Article Title: Two Iowa farmers gave up pigs and started growing mushrooms; their abandoned livestock buildings became an artisan food business
Article Text:
From pigs to mushrooms : Iowa farmers' big switch

Tanner Faaborg pushes for a new direction

The mushroom experiment begins

How an old hog barn became a mushroom farm

From fresh mushrooms to artisan food products

A manure pit becomes a wildlife pond

The money behind the transition

1100 Farm becomes a demonstration hub

Two Iowa farmers have transformed their family's former hog operation into a speciality mushroom business, turning infrastructure once built for thousands of pigs into spaces for growing lion's mane and oyster mushrooms. The Faaborg family, which once raised about 8,000 hogs a year, ended its animal-farming contract in October 2022 after decades in the industry. Their operation, now called 1100 Farm, has repurposed half of a 200-foot hog barn into mushroom-growing and processing space, while a former manure pit has been converted into a freshwater pond. With support from the Transfarmation Project, the family has expanded into value-added products including mushroom tinctures, flavoured salts, coffee and hot chocolate.The Faaborg family's move away from pigs followed decades of involvement in Iowa's livestock industry. Rand and Tammy Faaborg began raising pigs as a side business after buying their 25-acre farm. The operation eventually expanded through contract feeding, in which an integrator supplies animals and feed while farmers provide the buildings and labour.The family initially adapted existing structures to hold about 2,000 hogs.Later, they borrowed more than $400,000 to construct two larger hog barns. Rand said it took roughly 12 years to repay the debt.At its peak, the family operation was raising around 8,000 hogs annually. But the economics and demands of the business changed. Rand, who also worked as a welder, described periods when he worked 16-hour days and sometimes 24-hour stretches. He said that over 35 years, his income from his main job increased significantly, while his earnings from raising hogs declined by about two-thirds.The idea of changing the farm's direction gained momentum with the family's next generation. Their son Tanner Faaborg developed an interest in sustainability and climate issues while studying at college.After returning home, Tanner found himself caught between his interest in environmental issues and the realities of the family's hog operation. He began looking for ways to use the existing farm infrastructure without continuing to raise large numbers of animals.The family eventually began working with the Transfarmation Project in 2021, an initiative that helps farmers explore alternatives to intensive animal agriculture. The Faaborgs ended their animal-farming contract on October 23, 2022, according to the project's timeline.Mushrooms emerged as one possible alternative because they could be grown indoors using existing agricultural buildings. In 2023, the family received a $15,000 research and innovation grant to experiment with mushroom production and develop products.The family reported spending about $35,000 on site preparation, equipment and supplies, as well as branding and website development for the pilot.They began experimenting with speciality varieties, including lion's mane and oyster mushrooms. Instead of buying all their growing material, the family also learned to make its own mushroom blocks using soy hulls and hardwood pellets.The first mushroom crop was harvested and sold in March 2024, according to the Transfarmation Project's timeline.The family's new business is called 1100 Farm, a name linked to the capacity of the original hog barns.Rather than demolishing the old structures, the Faaborgs began converting them. By 2026, half of one approximately 200-foot-long hog barn had been transformed into a mushroom-growing facility.The renovated space includes specialised fruiting rooms where mushrooms grow under controlled conditions. Other areas are used for preparing growing substrate, developing mushroom spawn and processing the crop.The family has also discussed using the second hog barn for another agricultural venture. One possibility is growing microgreens, although that plan has not yet been implemented.The Faaborgs have not limited the business to selling fresh mushrooms. They have developed a range of value-added products designed to give the crop a longer shelf life and create additional revenue streams.1100 Farm currently sells products including lion's mane and reishi tinctures, mushroom salt, lion's mane coffee and lion's mane dark hot chocolate.The family is also working towards expanding its fresh-mushroom sales as production grows. The approach means the former livestock operation is now serving a different type of food market, combining farming with small-scale food processing and direct-to-consumer sales. A 2025 feature in The New York Times significantly boosted 1100 Farm's sales, with the Transfarmation Project reporting nearly 1,000 orders in the days after publication.The transformation has extended beyond the buildings. A former manure pit that once stored roughly one million gallons of liquid hog manure has been remediated and converted into a freshwater pond.Funding from the US Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service helped support the work.The family says the pond has attracted frogs, ducks and other wildlife. They have also planted native grasses and wildflowers and added trees and shrubs around parts of the property.The change illustrates how the family has repurposed not only its buildings but also other infrastructure associated with the former livestock operation.The Faaborgs' transition has involved several different sources of funding and financial commitments.The family received the $15,000 mushroom research grant in 2023 and reported spending around $35,000 on the pilot. Separately, Transfarmation has a $216,000 four-year contract with the family to document the transition, including costs, labour hours and product margins.The $216,000 is not the reported valuation or annual revenue of 1100 Farm. The family has not publicly disclosed a current business valuation or annual revenue figure.The original hog operation also involved significant borrowing. The family borrowed more than $400,000 to build its two larger hog barns, with Rand saying it took about 12 years to pay that debt.The Faaborg farm has since taken on a role beyond its own business. In July 2026, it became the Transfarmation Project's second demonstration hub.The site is intended to show farmers how existing livestock infrastructure can be adapted for other forms of agriculture. It also provides an opportunity to gather information about the practical costs and challenges involved in changing a farm's business model. The family is continuing to develop the mushroom operation while considering additional uses for the remaining livestock infrastructure.
Article Summary: The Faaborg family's move away from pigs followed decades of involvement in Iowa's livestock industry. At its peak, the family operation was raising around 8,000 hogs annually. The family's new business is called 1100 Farm, a name linked to the capacity of the original hog barns. A former manure pit has been converted into a freshwater pond.

Article Title: Pope vs Anthropic: Why 'AI consciousness' is dividing Silicon Valley and Vatican
Article Text:
The dispute points to a much bigger question surrounding the rapid development of AI.

What did Pope Leo XIV say about AI

Why is Anthropic thinking about AI's moral status

Anthropic's attempt to decide what AI should value

A debate over whether artificial intelligence could have something resembling consciousness has put Anthropic, one of the world's leading AI companies, at odds with the Vatican after Pope Leo XIV rejected the idea that machines could replace or surpass human beings.The disagreement surfaced after Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah reviewed the Pope's first encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas", ahead of its launch at the Vatican. Olah had accepted an invitation to speak at the event on May 25, but reportedly considered pulling Anthropic out after disagreeing with the Pope's position on AI consciousness.The dispute points to a much bigger question surrounding the rapid development of AI. As companies build increasingly capable systems and deploy them in everyday life, there is still disagreement over whether these systems should be understood simply as tools, autonomous agents or something closer to beings.In his encyclical, Leo warned against allowing technology to become more important than human beings." ... humanity — in all its grandeur and woundedness — must never be replaced or surpassed"He also wrote, "If technology becomes the ultimate criterion, the human person risks being reduced to data, a cog in a machine or a commodity."The Pope's position clashes with questions Olah has been raising privately about whether advanced AI systems could possess some form of moral status.According to The New York Times, Olah has encouraged religious thinkers to consider the possibility that Anthropic's Claude models could have something resembling moral status.Anthropic has spent months consulting religious scholars and other experts about how AI systems should behave and what values they should follow. The company has held private discussions with scholars from around the world and required participants to sign nondisclosure agreements, according to the Times.The effort comes as Anthropic pursues rapid expansion, with the company potentially reaching a valuation of $2 trillion.Olah has argued that AI development cannot be separated from questions about values and morality."Those who control AI will impose their own moral vision, which will become the invisible infrastructure of these systems," Olah argued, per the Times.His concerns go beyond philosophical questions. Anthropic has been examining possible real-world risks from AI, including disruption to jobs, cyberattacks and biological threats.AI systems are already being introduced into workplaces, customer services, search, education and other areas where their decisions can affect people's lives.Anthropic says it is trying to address these concerns through outside consultation and a written "constitution" for Claude.The 84-page document is intended to guide how the AI model behaves. The company has also consulted philosophers, religious scholars, psychologists and civil society representatives.Anthropic's in-house philosopher Amanda Askell said she wants the company's models to be "the best of us". Olah, meanwhile, has argued for "some shared notion of goodness that cuts across society in some very broad way," according to the Times.But questions remain over who should ultimately decide what values powerful AI systems should follow. Private discussions between technology companies and outside experts may influence AI behaviour, but they do not amount to public oversight.Olah has also said researchers are encountering behaviour in AI systems that they do not fully understand."I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling. We find structures that mirror results from human neuroscience. We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease. I don't know what that means, but I think it warrants ongoing discernment," Olah said, according to the Times.At the centre of the dispute is therefore a question that goes beyond the Vatican and Anthropic. As AI becomes more capable and increasingly embedded in society, researchers, technology companies and religious thinkers are still debating what these systems actually are, what rights or moral status they might have, and who should decide the values that guide them.
Article Summary: Pope Leo XIV rejected the idea that machines could replace or surpass human beings. The disagreement surfaced after Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah reviewed the Pope's first encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas" Olah has argued that AI development cannot be separated from questions about values and morality.

Article Title: Camp David huddle: Trump team discusses Iran war, possible Yemen offensive - report
Article Text:
File photo: Houthi supporters shout slogans during a rally against Israel and the United States' war on Iran, in Sanaa, Yemen

Iran talks and a possible return to combat

US president Donald Trump’s top national security aides met secretly at Camp David on Friday for several hours to discuss the war with Iran and the Saudi-backed push against Houthi rebels in Yemen, three US officials told Axios.The meeting was not announced by the Trump administration and came as negotiations with Iran remained stalled, with Trump weighing whether to resume major combat operations against Tehran.Vice president JD Vance chaired the meeting, according to the officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen Dan Caine were among those who attended.“Things were decided or at least deeply discussed,” one US official said, referring to the Middle East crisis.The White House did not comment on the meeting.The meeting came as Trump faces a decision over the future of the US campaign against Iran.With negotiations stalled, Trump has been considering whether to resume major combat operations. On Thursday, he issued a stark warning over the talks, saying: “Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won’t exist any longer.”Trump was asked about his next move on Iran on Friday afternoon while his advisers were meeting at Camp David.“If I told you, you would have a major story,” Trump told reporters. “But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well.”The Camp David discussions also covered the escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen.Saudi Arabia is preparing a possible offensive against the Houthis and has been urging Trump to support the campaign with US airstrikes.Trump has so far been leaning against joining the operation, although US officials said he could change his position.The meeting was notable because such high-level discussions at Camp David have been rare. A similar gathering took place in June 2025, days before Israel went to war with Iran.
Article Summary: Donald Trump's top national security aides met secretly at Camp David on Friday for several hours. Vice president JD Vance chaired the meeting, according to officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen Dan Caine were among those who attended.

Article Title: Texas woman kills 4-yr-old daughter, then shoots self dead after losing custody battle to ex-husband
Article Text:
Aaron's family said Vivian was supposed to return home to her father that evening. (Photo credit: X/Eric Daugherty)

A Texas mother allegedly killed her four-year-old daughter in an apparent murder-suicide, just hours after a court granted primary custody of the child to her father, who said she was “supposed to come home to him that evening”.Cibelle Savella, 35, was supposed to hand over her daughter, Vivian, to her ex-husband, Aaron Savella, on Tuesday evening. Instead, she fatally shot the child at their Houston home before turning the gun on herself, according to the Houston Police Department and family attorneys.Police were called to the residence at around 5:45pm and found Vivian dead and Cibelle with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound on the third floor. She was taken to a hospital but died a day later, police said, the New York Post reported.In a statement released through his attorney Stefani Shapiro, Aaron's family said Vivian was supposed to return home to her father that evening.“Our family is devastated. Vivian was four years old. She was loved without limit by her father, Aaron, and by everyone whose life she touched. There are no words for what has been taken from us,” the statement said.“Aaron did everything the law asks of a parent who is trying to protect his child. He trusted the courts. He followed every order. He waited for the process to work. On Tuesday, a judge placed Vivian in his primary care, and she was supposed to come home to him that evening. She never did,” it added.Cibelle's new husband, restaurateur Greg Kubala, and a babysitter were inside the house when the shots were fired, according to police and local media reports. They are not believed to have been involved in the shootings, the NY Post reported.“There was a custody hearing earlier today that didn’t go well for the mother,” Houston Police Lieutenant Larry Crowson said after the incident.The statement also said that the stories of “fathers who fight quietly, patiently, and within the law to protect their children, their stories are rarely told.”Shapiro said Aaron had never alleged that Cibelle physically abused Vivian but believed the child was “potentially being emotionally abused”.Cibelle, who was originally from Brazil, divorced Aaron in November 2024 after four years of marriage. The couple subsequently became involved in a legal dispute over custody of their daughter.According to court documents cited by US media, Aaron was granted exclusive rights to make decisions about Vivian's care. Cibelle was allowed to spend time with the child only under supervision by a Texas-based organisation.The court also imposed restrictions on Cibelle's involvement in Vivian's school activities and medical decisions. She was ordered to pay child support and contribute to half of her daughter's out-of-pocket medical expenses.According to reports citing court filings, Cibelle was also restricted from speaking to Vivian in Portuguese unless a supervisor present during the visit was fluent in the language. It was not immediately clear why the court imposed the restrictions.The circumstances surrounding the shootings remain under investigation.
Article Summary: Cibelle Savella, 35, was supposed to hand over her daughter, Vivian, to her ex- husband on Tuesday evening. Instead, she fatally shot the child at their Houston home before turning the gun on herself. Police were called to the residence at around 5:45pm and found Vivian dead.

Article Title: In 1938, a Texas family bought a ranch near Austin; 87 years later, a 202-acre conservation deal added protection to a 6,600-acre landscape that holds 10% of the Barton Creek watershed
Article Text:
Shield Ranch Barton CreekPhoto credit: @jvailphotography/ Instagram

A childhood shaped by wild land

Shield Ranch as the lungs of Barton Creek

Photo: Shield Ranch website

Layers of protection over decades

What the easements allow and prohibit

A camp that keeps the spirit alive

Why this matters for Austin’s water

A family legacy of stewardship

In 1938, Fred and Vera Shield of San Antonio bought a 5,300 acres on Barton Creek, beginning a multigenerational commitment to the land. Roughly, nine decades later, that same family has added another layer of protection through a 202-acre conservation easement with the City of Austin. The agreement, announced in 2026, is part of a broader strategy to safeguard Shield Ranch, a 6,600-acre wildland that contains about 10 percent of the Barton Creek watershed and plays a vital role in the region’s water quality, according to The Nature Conservancy and Shield Ranch. A portion of the easement’s appraised value was purchased using funds from the city’s 2018 Water Quality Protection Lands Bond, with the balance donated by the Shield-Ayres-Bowen family, according to a report by Shield Ranch.Vera Ayres Bowen and her brother Bob Ayres grew up spending long summers at the ranch their grandparents, Fred and Vera Shield, bought in 1938. Every trip from San Antonio began with a shared meal with the couple who lived on the property and helped work the land. After that, the children were free to roam, picking peaches and pears from trees planted by their grandparents and hiking through clusters of Ashe juniper and oak.Bowen recalls discovering armadillos and snakes, riding a horse alone through the undeveloped landscape, and leaping off a boulder into the family swimming hole in Barton Creek. Those experiences, she says, gave her a sense of independence and confidence that stayed with her into adulthood. The joy and freedom she felt on the ranch ultimately inspired the family to protect the land for future generations through conservation easements, as per a report by The Nature Conservancy.Shield Ranch encompasses 6,600 acres of protected wildlands ringed by hills and teeming with wildlife. The property is designated a Quiet Place by Quiet Parks International and is home to endangered golden-cheeked warblers. Six miles of Barton Creek wind through the ranch, which is also listed as a historic district in the National Register.Jeff Francell, associate director of land protection for The Nature Conservancy in Texas, describes Shield Ranch as the lungs of Barton Creek. He notes that if the Ayres family had chosen a different path, the area could have become a large master-planned community with serious negative effects on water quality. The fact that it will remain relatively undeveloped forever helps preserve the clarity and health of Barton Creek, the report by The Nature Conservancy further shared.The family’s conservation journey began in earnest after they developed their first ranch masterplan in the 1980s. They reached out to The Nature Conservancy in Texas to learn how they could protect the land, and the organisation served as a thought partner over the next decade. In the late 1990s, the Ayres family donated an easement on 4,670 acres to The Nature Conservancy, restricting certain types of development, as per Shield Ranch.They later sold an easement on an additional 1,676 acres to the City of Austin as part of its first voter-approved water protection program. The most recent 202-acre easement, announced in 2026, completes another chapter in this long-term strategy. A portion of the appraised value was purchased by the city using funds from the 2018 Water Quality Protection Lands Bond, while the balance was donated by the Shield-Ayres-Bowen family, as per the report.The conservation easements prohibit commercial development while allowing agricultural and recreational activities to continue. Limited development is permitted within strict parameters, including a small number of family residences and facilities for nonprofit organisations. This structure enables the family to maintain its stewardship role while ensuring the land’s ecological and hydrological functions remain intact.Under the terms of the agreements, officials from The Nature Conservancy and the City of Austin visit the property at least once a year to verify compliance. They also help troubleshoot any issues that arise on the ground. Bowen describes these agencies as great partners and says the family has benefited from their expertise and support over the years, as per reports.A 131-acre portion of the ranch is held by the nonprofit Shield Ranch Foundation, which operates Camp El Ranchito for youth who might not otherwise have access to outdoor programming. The camp moved into permanent, off-the-grid structures in 2022 and 2023, including a covered pavilion, rainwater collection tanks, evaporative toilets, and 11 sleeping shelters with walls that slide open to let in the breeze.The foundation works with organisations such as El Buen Samaritano and Westcave Outdoor Discovery Center to recruit students from fourth through twelfth grade. Bowen says her hope is that these campers will feel a kinship with the earth and become comfortable in nature, just as she and her siblings did as children. A stone monument on the site honours Indigenous people, European settlers, and ranchers who lived on the land before them, as per reports.Barton Creek is a key contributor to Barton Springs, a beloved natural resource and drinking water source for the Austin area. As the city grows rapidly, pressure on surrounding land has increased. Shield Ranch sits in a zone where large-scale development could compromise water quality, hydrologic function, and biodiversity. The easements help ensure that this portion of the watershed remains a buffer against urban runoff and habitat loss.City leaders describe the ranch as part of a network of protected open space that represents a generational investment by Austin citizens. Voters have repeatedly approved taxpayer funds to permanently protect Barton Creek’s water quality, wildlife habitat, and open space. The 202-acre easement marks the completion of the 2018 bond program, which funded the permanent protection of more than 6,830 acres across the recharge and contributing zones for Barton Springs.Patricia Shield Ayres, co-owner of Shield Ranch, says her family has been committed to land stewardship and natural resource conservation for nearly 90 years. The first conservation easement was donated in 1998, and each subsequent agreement reflects an ongoing commitment to safeguarding highly developable land along Barton Creek. Today, Shield Ranch Barton Creek is protected through three easements, one held by The Nature Conservancy and two by the City of Austin, as per Shield Ranch's website.Bowen frames the family’s role as one of temporary caretakers in a long line of stewards. She says their work was about caring for the land during their time and using tools like conservation easements to ensure it would remain wild for those who come after. Her hope is that 50 or 100 years from now, the ranch will look much as it does today, a rare and truly wild place in an increasingly urban region.
Article Summary: Shield Ranch is a 6,600-acre wildland that contains about 10 percent of the Barton Creek watershed and plays a vital role in the region’s water quality. Fred and Vera Shield of San Antonio bought a 5,300 acres on Barton Creek in 1938, beginning a multigenerational commitment to the land. The family has added another layer of protection through a 202-acre conservation easement with the City of Austin.

Article Title: Pakistan logs over 1.2k rebel attacks in 9 months of ’26, security crisis deepens
Article Text: During the first nine months of 2026, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks, according to a report by Islamabad-based think tank Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, indicating that a major security crisis is brewing. The number of attacks in Sept reached a 12-year high, with 225 attacks resulting in 545 deaths. Police and military personnel have been the primary targets of these operations, accounting for majority of fatalities.Spearheaded by groups such as Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), Baloch Liberation Army, Baloch Liberation Front and alliances like Ittehad Mujahideen Pakistan, these attacks remain concentrated in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and former tribal areas. Formed in 2025, IMP is the latest threat and comprises three sub-outfits — Hafiz Gul Bahadur group (HGBG), Lashkar-e-Islam and Harakat Inqilab-e-Islami Pakistan.Just last week, over a dozen security personnel were killed and at least 30 wounded in a suicide bombing at a roadside police checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. A week before that around 21 Pakistani security personnel were killed and dozens injured in a powerful suicide bombing and subsequent firing at the police line and intelligence facility in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The surge in Sept represents a 13% increase from 199 incidents reported in Aug, marking the third consecutive month of compounding violence.Balochistan served as the primary epicentre of the escalation, bearing the brunt of the violence with 131 recorded attacks, accounting for more than half of all nationwide incidents. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa followed with 58 attacks, while the former tribal areas recorded 34 incidents, the institute claimed. Tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have risen as Pakistan repeatedly accuses the ruling Afghan Taliban of providing safe havens and operational freedom to the TTP.
Article Summary: During the first nine months of 2026, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks. The number of attacks in Sept reached a 12-year high, with 225 attacks resulting in 545 deaths. Police and military personnel have been the primary targets of these operations.

Article Title: Shehbaz govt, Imran Khan’s PTI hold talks as Pakistan braces for protests
Article Text: Pakistan’s federal government and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) agreed to hold a second round of talks on Saturday, as the opposition party prepares for a long march towards Islamabad from October 4.The first round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, who is facilitating the dialogue amid heightened security in the capital.According to a statement issued by the National Assembly Secretariat, the participants held detailed discussions “on the prevailing political situation and exchanged views on various matters of national importance”.“The government, PPP and opposition representatives apprised each other of their respective positions and held a detailed exchange of views constructively and cordially. The participants emphasised the need to resolve national issues through dialogue and negotiations,” it said, according to news agency PTI.The second round will be held at 2 pm on Saturday in the speaker’s chamber.Sadiq said he was “only playing the role of a mediator”, adding that his office was “always open” to resolving issues through negotiations.“Parliament is the only forum where solutions to issues can be found,” he said, stressing that negotiations were the way to address political differences.PTI international spokesman Zulfiqar Bukhari said the talks were “primarily aimed at defusing the current political situation surrounding PTI’s planned march/protest toward Islamabad on October 4”.Bukhari said the party’s demands included an “immediate” meeting with Khan and a decision to take him to hospital so his personal doctors could examine him. PTI has also sought the release of Khan’s sisters and others arrested ahead of the protest, a medical check-up for his wife Bushra Bibi and proper hearings in their cases.Meanwhile, the Pakistan authorities have deployed additional police and placed shipping containers on routes into Islamabad. The blockades have already disrupted freight movement.Bukhari said the long march would begin from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat, with stops planned in Karak and Kohat on October 5 before entering Peshawar district.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf to hold second round of talks on Saturday. Opposition party preparing for long march towards Islamabad from October 4. First round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq.

Article Title: 'Vague and broad': UN experts slam Pakistan's counter-terrorism laws, demand release of lawyer couple
Article Text:
UN experts demand release of Pakistani lawyers, question terror laws

United Nations human rights experts have stepped up pressure on Pakistan to release Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha, after the married couple was rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail on September 17.The Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that the latest charges relate to an earlier case dating back to March 2025, when the two lawyers were accused in connection with their participation in a protest that authorities deemed illegal.The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists and criticised the military.They said the decision to invoke an older case immediately after Mazari-Hazir and Chattha secured bail “appears to be an attempt” to use the criminal justice system to punish freedom of expression and human rights advocacy.The couple’s rearrest was followed by proceedings before an Islamabad anti-terrorism court. Police had sought 30 days of custody for interrogation, but the court rejected the request and ordered that the lawyers be sent to jail on a 14-day judicial remand, OHCHR said.Their legal proceedings continued on September 22, when an Islamabad anti-terrorism court returned their bail petitions because they did not carry signed powers of attorney, according to the UN rights office.The UN experts also raised broader concerns about Pakistan’s use of counter-terrorism legislation, criticising what they described as “vague and broad” provisions that could be used to restrict human rights and interfere with legitimate advocacy.They called on Pakistani authorities to drop any charges stemming from the lawyers’ exercise of freedom of expression or their legitimate professional work.The experts also urged authorities to ensure that the couple had access to lawyers of their choice, their families and necessary medical care.The UN experts said they had been in contact with the Pakistani government over their concerns.
Article Summary: Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha were rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail. The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists.

Article Title: Policeman killed in gunmen attack in Pakistan’s khyber pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
A police officer was killed in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

A police officer was killed in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province after two armed med riding a motorcycle attacked him with a hand grenede and fired at him while he was deployed outside a hospital, police said.The attack took place in the unstable province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Tank area.The banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) later claimed the responsibility for the attack, as per the PTI report.According to the police, the two attackers escaped from the spot on their motorcyclen after the attackSecurity personnel have launched a search operation to trace the assailants, while an investigation into the incident is also in progress.Over the years, there have been several instances of terrorist violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which shares a border with Afghanistan. The transfer of combatants across borders and subsequent military actions have also been connected to the disturbance.The TTP has continued to carry out attacks in the province since its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government ended in November
Article Summary: The attack took place in the unstable province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Tank area. The banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) later claimed responsibility for the attack. The TTP has continued to carry out attacks in the province since its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government ended in November.

Article Title: Pakistan forces kill 7 TTP militants in North Waziristan amid rising violence along Afghan border
Article Text:
Pakistan military-led government refers to the banned TTP as Fitna al Khawarij.

Seven militants belonging to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed by security forces during an intelligence-based operation in north-western Pakistan on Friday, according to an official.The operation took place in Eidak, an area of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which has witnessed repeated militant attacks in recent years.Security forces also destroyed several hideouts during the operation, the official said. The action was carried out under the government's Azm-e-Istehkam move, which is part of Pakistan's purported efforts to tackle terrorism.Pakistan's federal government refers to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, as Fitna al Khawarij.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has remained a major hotspot for militant violence, partly because of its border with Afghanistan. The region has also seen repeated military operations and the movement of fighters across the border.The TTP ended its ceasefire with the Pakistani military-led government in November 2022. Since then, the group has carried out repeated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, particularly against security forces.Figures from the Centre for Research and Security Studies show that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was Pakistan's worst-hit region for violence in the third quarter of 2025.It recorded 638 violence-related deaths, accounting for nearly 71 per cent of the national total, along with 221 violent incidents, or more than 67 per cent of the total.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, both of which border Afghanistan, together accounted for more than 96 per cent of militant-related violence recorded in Pakistan during that period.Separately, Reuters sources reported an attack on a convoy of paramilitary troops in the volatile Kurram district. Roadside bombs struck the convoy before a large group of militants opened fire, according to five Pakistani security officials.The Pakistani Taliban claimed responsibility for that attack in a statement to a Reuters reporter. Pakistan's military public relations wing did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Security forces launched a search operation to locate those responsible, while the government had not issued an official statement at the time of the report.The TTP has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in recent months. The group seeks to overthrow the Pakistani government and establish its own hardline interpretation of Islamic rule.Islamabad has accused Afghanistan of allowing the TTP to use its territory to train fighters and plan attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul has denied the allegation.
Article Summary: Seven militants belonging to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed by security forces during an intelligence-based operation. The operation took place in Eidak, an area of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Security forces also destroyed several hideouts during the operation, the official said.

Article Title: Jail, isolation, crackdown: Why Pakistan’s establishment has failed to break Imran Khan
Article Text:
Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023 (File photo)

How Imran Khan got here

Why Imran Khan matters

Imran Khan: From cricket captain to PM to inmate

How state failed to marginalise Imran Khan politically

Imran Khan: PTI's 'red line'

The 'persecution' of Imran Khan

Main legal cases against Imran Khan

Imran Khan: A case that resonates beyond politics

The state’s struggle to marginalise Imran Khan

Islamabad had prepared for another confrontation. Roads were blocked, security forces deployed and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters were expected to march towards the capital demanding the release of their jailed leader, Imran Khan Then, days before the September 27 protest, PTI postponed the march until October 4, temporarily easing the pressure on the government.But the roads can be reopened and the barricades removed. The political problem surrounding Imran Khan is proving harder to clear.The former prime minister has now spent more than three years behind bars. The establishment has used imprisonment, restrictions on his contact with the outside world, scores of legal cases and a crackdown on his supporters. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics. PTI-backed independents won the largest number of directly elected national assembly seats in the 2024 general election, and his supporters continue to mobilise around demands for his release.The postponed Islamabad march is therefore less an end to the latest confrontation than another pause in a political standoff that has survived elections, convictions and imprisonment.Imran Khan retired from international cricket in 1992, shortly after leading Pakistan to its first and, so far, only 50-over Cricket World Cup title. Four years later, in 1996, he formally entered politics by founding the PTI.His political breakthrough finally came after the 2018 general election, when the PTI emerged as the single-largest party and he became prime minister. His rise to power was widely seen by rivals and analysts as having benefited from the backing of Pakistan’s military, the country’s most powerful institution, although both Khan and the military denied that the army had helped bring him to power.That relationship subsequently deteriorated. In April 2022, the opposition brought a parliamentary no-confidence vote against Imran Khan, which he lost and was thus removed from office.He has since faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged, while he has consistently denied wrongdoing.Imran Khan was imprisoned in August 2023 and has remained behind bars since then. Yet his incarceration has done little to diminish his presence in Pakistan’s public life or erase him from the public consciousness.Thanks to his cricket career, Imran Khan was already a well-known public figure before entering politics. Following his retirement, he gained further goodwill by giving Pakistan its first specialised cancer hospital, the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, named after his mother, in Lahore. The hospital opened in 1994.That personal following later became the foundation of a political movement, the PTI, that presented him as an outsider challenging Pakistan’s established political order. In a country where civilian politics has long been shaped by the Bhutto-Zardari and Sharif families, Imran Khan offered voters a figure outside the traditional political dynasties. His image as a retired cricket captain with no family legacy in politics helped distinguish him from the established political class.His prime ministership brought him further visibility and established him as a central figure in Pakistan’s civilian politics.And therein lies his significance: an outsider who challenged Pakistan’s established political dynasties, became prime minister, and later fell out with the military establishment before being jailed.Pakistan’s 2024 general election offered the clearest indication that Imran Khan’s imprisonment had not erased his political relevance. Despite the PTI being stripped of its election symbol and Imran Khan remaining in prison, PTI-backed independents won 92 directly elected National Assembly seats — more than candidates backed by any other political grouping.While that result did not bring the party back to power, it showed that his absence from the ballot did not translate into the disappearance of his support.However, the outcome should not have been a surprise. In October 2022, just months after his ouster as prime minister, Imran Khan contested by-elections in seven of eight National Assembly constituencies voting on October 16. He won six of the seven seats he contested, while the Pakistan People’s Party won the other two constituencies.He then won another by-election in Kurram on October 30, taking his tally of by-election victories that month to seven.The by-election results offered an early indication that removing Imran Khan from office had not dented his electoral support. The 2024 elections reinforced that point, showing that his imprisonment and the restrictions placed on the PTI had not eliminated its support among voters.As its founder and most prominent face, PTI has repeatedly described Imran Khan as its “red line.” The phrase took on greater significance after his arrest on May 9, 2023, when Pakistan witnessed widespread rioting and arson by PTI supporters. Protesters targeted government buildings and military installations, including the residence of a corps commander in Lahore and the army’s general headquarters in Rawalpindi.The events marked a dramatic escalation in the confrontation between Imran Khan and the military establishment. They also demonstrated why the PTI has continued to place him at the centre of its politics: attempts to remove him from the political arena have not removed the attachment to him among a significant section of the party’s supporters.Since his incarceration, the party has repeatedly mobilised in Islamabad, demanding his release. The federal government’s frustration with these protests was evident ahead of the recently postponed Islamabad march, when interior minister Mohsin Naqvi spoke of the need to find a “permanent solution” to the PTI’s repeated demonstrations in the capital.“This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway,” Naqvi said.Therefore, Imran Khan remains the PTI’s “red line” — one reason efforts to marginalise him politically have so far struggled to succeed.Imran Khan’s prolonged imprisonment has also strengthened a persecution narrative around him. His party and supporters have consistently argued that the numerous cases against him are politically motivated and intended to keep him out of politics. Pakistani authorities have rejected those allegations.The fact that more than 100 cases have been brought against him, his disqualification by the Election Commission in 2022, and the restrictions imposed on the PTI ahead of the 2024 general elections have only strengthened that narrative among his supporters.The conditions of his imprisonment at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail have added another dimension to the persecution narrative.In December 2025, UN Special Rapporteur on torture Alice Jill Edwards raised concerns over reports that Khan was being held in conditions falling below international standards for humane and dignified detention. The communication cited allegations of prolonged solitary confinement, restricted access to the outside world and inadequate ventilation.Edwards subsequently urged Pakistani authorities to end his reported solitary confinement and ensure that his detention conditions complied with international standards, warning that the reported conditions could amount to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment.The Pakistani establishment has succeeded in keeping Imran Khan behind bars. But with so many eyes on his case, it has not succeeded in making his political relevance disappear.The controversy surrounding Imran Khan’s imprisonment has increasingly extended beyond politics and Pakistan, as his cricketing legacy has kept his case in the international spotlight.Former international cricket captains have appealed to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government over Khan’s treatment and access to medical care. In August, 21 former captains urged the government to ensure “humane treatment and proper medical care” for their former on-field rival.Matters almost came to a head during the recent England-Pakistan Test series. During the second Test at Lord’s, the Pakistan Cricket Board reportedly considered not sending its players back onto the field after the lunch break after Sky Sports aired an interview with Imran Khan’s sons, Kasim and Suleiman.The PCB ultimately returned to the field and lodged a complaint with the broadcaster.The episode underscored how Imran Khan’s imprisonment continues to attract attention beyond Pakistan and outside politics.Every time the PTI has marched on Islamabad, the Pakistan government has responded by fortifying the capital, blocking entry routes and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.Ahead of the September 27 march, authorities deployed thousands of security personnel and erected extensive barricades and roadblocks around Islamabad.The crackdown extended to Imran Khan’s family too, with his three sisters detained ahead of the now-postponed march.Such measures may prevent protesters from reaching Islamabad, but they have not stopped the PTI from returning to the streets with the same central demand: Imran Khan’s release. The state has managed to contain individual protests, but each confrontation has been followed by another, keeping his imprisonment at the centre of Pakistan’s politics.By isolating him in prison and cracking down on his family and party, the Pakistani authorities have sought to contain Imran Khan’s political influence. So far, however, his electoral support, PTI’s continued mobilisation and the attention surrounding his imprisonment show that those measures have not removed him from the country’s political contest.For now, Imran Khan’s ability to retain political relevance despite his imprisonment remains a significant feature of Pakistan’s politics.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023. He has faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics.

Article Title: BLF’s newly-formed female unit 'KAAD' attacks military convoy in Balochistan; claims nine killed
Article Text:
Image credit: X

The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has released footage of an attack by its newly formed female unit on a Pakistani military convoy in Turbat, claiming that nine security personnel were killed in the operation.The video, released through the group’s media cell Aashoob, shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway on September 22.The footage includes a female commander briefing fighters before the operation, along with training clips. It also shows the fighters opening fire on the convoy from close range. The group claimed that several military vehicles were severely damaged and that several personnel were injured. These claims could not be independently verified.BLF spokesperson Major Gwahram Baloch said the group’s Qurban unit supported the operation and helped its fighters resist an attempt by Pakistani forces to encircle them, while covering their withdrawal. He said Qurban unit fighter Chakar Murad, alias Dileep Jan, was killed during the attack.The video also shows KAAD members conducting snap checks of vehicles in the Mangchar area of Kalat. The BLF claimed that its fighters carried out a blockade and vehicle checks there.In a separate incident, the Baloch Republican Army (BRA) claimed responsibility for an attack on a Mari Energies Limited site in the Beh Loti area of Dera Bugti, using rockets and heavy weapons.BRA spokesperson Sarbaz Baloch claimed that three company employees were killed and several others injured. He said a clash followed between Pakistani forces and members of a local armed group. The BRA claimed nine Pakistani military personnel and three members of the armed group were killed, while six of its own fighters also lost their lives, according to The Balochistan Post.The Baloch Republican Guards (BRG) separately claimed that its fighters seized Haji Shehr and destroyed a local police station using explosives. It also said BRA fighters entered Eri Shehr, took control of government facilities and withdrew after the operation.KAAD is named after Karima Baloch, a pro-independence activist and the first woman chairperson of the Baloch Students Organisation-Azad. She was found dead in Toronto in 2020.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) claims nine security personnel were killed in the operation. Video shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China- Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway.

Article Title: 'Technical issue': Pakistan blocks airspace for Russian flight carrying uranium for Bangladesh nuclear plant
Article Text:
Russia’s uranium shipment for Bangladesh’s Rooppur nuclear plant delayed (Image credit: Reuters)

Poll Vote & Share your view Should international diplomatic norms allow for expedited clearance of flights carrying critical supplies like nuclear fuel? Definitely Not at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Pakistan has denied airspace clearance to a Russian cargo flight carrying nuclear fuel for Bangladesh's Rooppur nuclear power plant, delaying the scheduled arrival of uranium for the facility's Unit 2. Pakistan later described the matter as a "technical and procedural" issue involving flight routing and airspace permissions.The nuclear fuel was scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on September 24 but did not reach the country after the aircraft was not allowed to use Pakistani airspace. Russia has now proposed the first week of October as a new arrival date, according to Bangladesh officials as cited by news agency ANI."We heard that a cargo plane carrying uranium for the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Bangladesh was scheduled to arrive on September 24. However, the flight was not given permission to use Pakistani airspace, so the uranium did not arrive in Bangladesh as planned. As of now, the exact reason for Pakistan not granting the airspace clearance is still unknown", ANI quoted Bangladesh's minister for science and technology Faqir Mahbub Anam saying."A new date has been proposed, with Russia indicating the first week of October for the uranium to arrive in Bangladesh", he added.Sheikh Mohammed Tauhidul Islam, joint secretary in Bangladesh's science and technology ministry, said preparations had been completed at the airport before officials were informed that the airspace was unavailable."We had completed all the preparations at the airport and were waiting, but the liaison officer from Rosatom told us that the airspace was not clear. So we couldn’t send it. It may need to be rescheduled", he said.Pakistan's high commission in Dhaka, in a clarification, said the matter was related to technical and procedural arrangements."Pakistan maintains an unwavering commitment to international diplomatic norms and processes all requests for diplomatic flight and overflight clearances within a standardised, predictable timeframe, strictly in accordance with our established regulatory guidelines and civil aviation protocols," ANI quoted it as saying."With regard to the reports being quoted, the matter appears to relate to technical and procedural arrangements concerning flight routing and airspace permissions, which can occasionally require coordination among the relevant aviation and other authorities and may result in adjustments to flight schedules", it added.The high commission also said the incident should not be linked to Pakistan-Bangladesh ties."Pakistan attaches high importance to its relations with Bangladesh, and it would therefore be appropriate to view the matter in its proper technical context and not attach undue significance to reports or narratives that may seek to misplace it to undermine our bilateral relations," it said.The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, Bangladesh's first nuclear power facility, is being built with technical assistance from Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom. The project comprises two VVER-1200 reactor units with a combined capacity of 2,400 MW.
Article Summary: The nuclear fuel was scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on September 24 but did not reach the country after the aircraft was not allowed to use Pakistani airspace. Pakistan later described the matter as a "technical and procedural" issue involving flight routing and airspace permissions. Russia has now proposed the first week of October as a new arrival date.

Article Title: 'Took mobile phones, cash': Karachi football team robbed at gunpoint on Balochistan highway
Article Text:
Image credit X @Baloch_Nojawan

NEW DELHI: A football team travelling from Karachi to Quetta to participate in the Chief Minister’s Gold Cup tournament was robbed at gunpoint on a highway in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, PTI reported on Monday.Around a dozen armed men intercepted the Karachi District West team’s bus between Mastung and Sariab, and took away the players’ mobile phones, cash and other valuables. The incident took place on Monday evening, leaving the players without money.Team manager Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto said the armed men ordered all passengers to get off the bus before robbing them."The armed men asked all the passengers to disembark from the bus and then took away all mobile phones, cash, and other valuables. They also butted some of the passengers."After reaching Quetta, the team informed Balochistan’s sports minister about the robbery. The minister intervened to provide the players with daily allowances, according to the report.Muhammad Azam, secretary of the Sindh Football Association, an affiliated unit of the Pakistan Football Federation, said the team had travelled despite official warnings against using road and rail routes to Quetta."We didn't send the Sindh team and we advised all other clubs in Karachi to avoid going to Quetta by bus or train because of the security situation. The Karachi west team still went ahead and what we feared happened," Muhammad Azam said.He added that the Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa football associations had also not sent teams for the tournament.The incident comes days after two local cricketers were abducted from Dera Bugti.The highway connecting Mastung district to Quetta has become a hotspot for armed groups targeting travellers, PTI reported.
Article Summary: A football team travelling from Karachi to Quetta was robbed at gunpoint. Around a dozen armed men intercepted the Karachi District West team’s bus. They took away the players’ mobile phones, cash and other valuables.

Article Title: Child, forced marriages of minority girls in Pakistan flagged at UN event
Article Text:
UN rights event highlights risks faced by girls in Pakistan’s child marriages (ANI photo)

The impact of child and forced marriages on girls in Pakistan, particularly those from minority communities, was discussed at a side event during the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva.Speakers at the event raised concerns about girls being married at a young age and the consequences for their education, health and basic rights. The event was reported by Global Human Rights Defence, a UN ECOSOC-accredited human rights organisation.Naveed Walter, president of Human Rights Focus Pakistan and a human rights defender, pointed to the scale of child rights violations in Pakistan and the vulnerability of children who enter marriage at an early age.“Most recently, UNICEF gave the data about Pakistan. Ninety million women and children and girls have been affected by child rights violations. And of them, 4.8 million were under 15 years of age,” Walter said.Walter said early marriage can leave girls without access to basic education and expose them to serious health risks, particularly during pregnancy.“You know, dear excellencies and dear audience, that during pregnancy, millions of children have died.And you know, under 30 per cent of the children who get married even have basic education,” he said.The discussion also focused on Sindh, where women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood.“According to the National Commission on the Rights of the Child, 84,000 children between the ages of 10 and 17 are married, widowed and separated. Many of them have already left school, and many face serious health risks,” Kandhro said.Kandhro said 21% of young women in Sindh had been married before turning 18. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.According to her, Pakistan sees an estimated 61,000 pregnancies among girls aged 15 to 19 each year. Only 44% of pregnant girls in this age group receive at least four antenatal visits, she said.Kandhro also cited anaemia among girls in Sindh, putting the figure at 61.9%. She described this as the highest rate among the provinces.The speakers urged stronger safeguards for women and children and called for greater international attention to child and forced marriage, which they linked to gender-based violence.
Article Summary: UN rights event highlights risks faced by girls in Pakistan’s child marriages. Women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.

Article Title: Motorcycle-borne gunmen kill 3 cops in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
TTP suspicion after 3 traffic cops killed in Pakistan gun attack (ANI file photo)

Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday, the Associated Press cited police.The attack took place in Wazirabad Bazaar in Tank district when suspected militants on motorcycles opened fire on a vehicle carrying the traffic police.The attackers fled the area after the shooting, local police official Jamshed Khan said.No group has claimed responsibility for the latest attack. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.The attack on police officials came two days after 'fidayeen' bomb blast in Dera Ismail Khan city in the same province. The suicide bombing killed at least 13 people and wounded over 30 others.Gunmen also opened fire on an ambulance that arrived at the scene. The TTP claimed responsibility for that attack.Pakistan has repeatedly accused Afghanistan’s Taliban government of allowing TTP militants to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks in Pakistan.Kabul has denied the allegations and said it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries.
Article Summary: Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.

Article Title: 20-year-old Azerbaijani woman allegedly drugged, gang-raped in Pakistan's Lahore
Article Text:
Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked (AP file photo)

A 20-year-old woman from Azerbaijan was allegedly gang-raped by three men in Lahore after being taken to a flat in the Defence Housing Authority area, news agency PTI cited police on Sunday.The incident allegedly took place after the woman, who came to Pakistan from Baku for business, was taken to a cafe by two women late on September 25. Police said three men joined them at the cafe around 11 pm and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.Instead, the men allegedly took the Azerbaijani woman to a flat, where they gave her an intoxicating substance and sexually assaulted her, according to police.She was later left near Lahore's Ghazi Interchange. The suspects allegedly took her iPhone before abandoning her.Police officer Anjum Bashir said the woman had been staying in Lahore's Raiwind area since arriving in Pakistan more than two weeks ago.Police have registered a case against three men and identified the main accused. Raids are being conducted to arrest the suspects, while their names have also been placed on the stop list to prevent them from leaving the country.The vehicle allegedly used in the incident has been recovered from the house of a relative of the main accused, Bashir said.Investigators are also examining the role of the two women who allegedly took the victim to the cafe.The woman has undergone a medical examination and police have registered the case under relevant provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code.
Article Summary: Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked. Incident allegedly took place after the woman was taken to a cafe by two women. Police said three men joined them at the cafe and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.

Article Title: 'Don't go back like this': Pakistan minister's throat-cut gesture to Afghan journalist backfires - video
Article Text:
Pak minister’s throat-cut gesture to Afghan journalist

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has faced criticism on social media over a threat-like gesture he made towards an Afghan woman journalist who questioned him about Pakistan's ties with the Taliban and its response to the treatment of Afghan women.The incident took place on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.The video clearly shows that journalist asked Asif what message Pakistan had for the Taliban over their policies toward Afghan women and why Islamabad had not challenged those policies when the Taliban were considered friends."What's your message to the Taliban now? To change their policy towards Afghan women? Why at the beginning, Pakistan didn't teach them that," the journalist asked, according to a video of the exchange shared on social media.Asif interrupted her without answering the question and pointed towards her attire."Don't go back like this over there. They will... otherwise they will..," he said, while making a hand gesture across his neck.The gesture drew strong condemnation online, with several social media users saying it appeared to imply that the journalist could be killed if she returned to Afghanistan. Users also criticised Asif and the men accompanying him for laughing after his remarks.A user on X wrote: "This is an utterly disgraceful way for a senior government minister to respond to a woman asking a serious question.""A woman asking about the suffering of Afghan women deserved an answer not intimidation, mockery, and laughter," he added.The journalist's question centred on the Taliban's policies towards Afghan women and Pakistan's position on them. Social media users said the response and the gesture were inappropriate and appeared to carry a threat of violence.The incident comes amid fresh tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with Islamabad carrying out aerial and drone strikes inside Afghanistan early Thursday.The Taliban also confirmed to news agency Reuters that 28 "fighters" were killed after crossing from Pakistan into eastern Afghanistan. The ruling-authority in Kabul also added that most of them were former Afghan security personnel.Pakistan called the strikes as "precision attacks" on 10 locations. Federal information minister Atauallah Tarar said the operation was carried out in response to drones launched from Afghanistan a day earlier.According to Dawn, Tarar said in a post on X that the strikes targeted locations allegedly used for launching and storing drones. He described the operation as "deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".Afghanistan has warned Pakistan of "dire consequences" over the strikes, describing them as blatant aggression."In this criminal aggression, four of our fellow Afghan compatriots have been martyred. The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan strongly condemns these blind and cowardly attacks in the harshest terms, considering them a flagrant violation of all principles, a blatant aggression, and a crime," Afghan government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said.Cross-border hostilities between the two neighbours have continued in recent weeks, with Pakistan carrying out military action, including aerial strikes, inside Afghanistan.
Article Summary: Pak defence minister Khawaja Asif made a threat-like gesture to an Afghan journalist. The journalist asked him about Pakistan's ties with the Taliban and its response to the treatment of Afghan women. Social media users said the response and the gesture were inappropriate and appeared to carry a threat of violence.

Article Title: At least 13 dead in suicide bomb blast near police post in northwestern Pakistan
Article Text:

Pakistani Taliban claims responsibility

(With AP inputs)

At least 13 people were killed and around 35 others wounded on Saturday when a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan, police and rescue officials said.The attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Local police chief Safdar Baloch said most of the injured were security personnel and passersby, with some in critical condition.According to Baloch, gunmen later opened fire on an ambulance carrying victims to a nearby hospital, killing a rescue worker and injuring two others.Two women and a child were also among those killed in the suicide bombing, he added.The Pakistan i Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 after the US withdrew its troops.Pakistan has witnessed a surge in militant attacks in recent years, many of them claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist group primarily active in neighbouring Balochistan province.Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and have demanded that Kabul prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Afghan authorities have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks against other countries.Dera Ismail Khan is near South Waziristan, a former militant stronghold where the Pakistani military has carried out several operations in recent years.In December 2023, a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at the main gate of a police station in Dera Ismail Khan, killing at least 23 security personnel in one of the deadliest attacks in the area. It was claimed by Tehreek-e-Jihad Pakistan, a small militant group believed to be an offshoot of the TTP.
Article Summary: The attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. The Pakistan i Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban.

Article Title: Pakistan govt puts Islamabad on lockdown as Imran Khan’s party pushes ahead with march
Article Text:
Islamabad locked down as PTI prepares for Imran Khan march

Leaders of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party have vowed to press ahead with nationwide demonstrations demanding his release, as authorities tightened security in Islamabad ahead of the planned march.More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads, while sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed across the city.The government has also deployed security personnel in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and closed the main highway linking the provincial capital, Peshawar, with Islamabad. The sweeping security measures have fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with several businesses struggling to receive supplies.The measures to prevent Khan’s PTI from proceeding with the march come amid mounting concerns over the treatment of the former prime minister, who has been in jail since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.On Friday, PTI leaders announced that they would postpone the start of the march to October 4, a week after the original September 27 date, saying they hoped the delay would put further pressure on the government.The planned protest also comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan’s sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were ordered to remain in custody for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.
Article Summary: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads. Sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed.
